10. Representation and Voting.

(a) The constitution or bylaws of local Central
bodies shall provide, among other things, for the
holding of meetings, the selection of delegates to
such meetings, and the basis of representation
therein. They shall provide for representation and
voting procedures on a basis which will be equita-
ble and which will assure the representative char-
acter of the local central body, and shall provide
for a roll-call vote on any pending question, in-
cluding elections, upon demand of a reasonable
fixed percentage or number of delegates, which
percentage or number shall not exceed thirty (30)
percent of the delegates present. The number of
votes to which a local union is entitled on roll-
calls shall be equal to, or directly proportional to,
the average membership of the local union as de-
ermined by the per capita tax payments to the
tral body for the preceding two calendar quar-
fers, or such longer reasonable period as the cen-
Hal body’s constitution may prescribe, but not to
exceed the number of months between elections.

11. Delegates.

(a) No person shall be eligible to serve as a
delegate to a local central body unless he is a
member of a local union affiliated with such local
central body or, if the constitution or bylaws of
the central body so provides, unless he is a na-
tional or international union representative regu-
larly servicing such a local union, nor shall any
person be eligible to serve as a delegate who holds
a salaried position, or any other position of ad-
ministrative or executive authority, in a union or

any subordinate branch of a union which has been
suspended or expelled from the AFL-CIO.
(b) No local central body shall reject creden-

tials presented by a duly elected or appointed
delegate who is eligible to be a delegate under

the provisions of paragraph (a) of this rule.

23. Publications and Advertising.

Experience has demonstrated that irresponsible
publishers of so-called labor papers, yearbooks
and directories and/or unscrupulous solicitors of
advertising for such publications and for so-called
advertising boards, have, on Occasion, exploited
the name and good reputation of the AFL-CIO
to further their own selfish ends, and to the detri-
ment of the best interests of organized labor.
Therefore, no local central body shall be asso-
ciated in any way with a so-called advertising
board, or with a yearbook or labor directory when

such yearbook or labor directory accepts com-
mercial advertising of any kind.

_ It should be clearly understood that labor pub-
lications should exist for the sole purpose of fur-
thering the best interests of the labor movement
not as a source of additional revenue. Therefore,

Dear Brother Davidoff:

This will acknowledge the charter application and the proposed
constitution for a new local central body, submitted by Regional
Director Mary Crayton, to be known as Mid-State Central Labor
Council (New York) with territorial jurisdiction over Cortland,
Tompkins and Schuyler Counties.

Also acknowledged is a check in the amount of $50.00 to cover
the cost of a new charter and seal.

In accordance with Rule 8 of the Rules Governing AFL-CIO Local
Central Bodies, the proposed constitution is hereby approved.

In accordance with Rule 5 of the Rules Governing AFL-CIO Local
Central Bodies, the issuance of a new charter is hereby approved.
The new charter and seal will be sent to you within forty-five
days.

With best wishes for the success of the Mid-State Central
Labor Council, I am

Sincerely and fraternally,

President

Dear Labor Coalition Member Union,

Enclosed you will find one (1) copy of the proposed
Constitution for affiliation with the National AFL-CIO
(additional copies are available from The Labor Coalition upon
request). This is the document which will be discussed and voted
on for ratification at our October 6th General Meeting.

Many hours of effort, by many people went into reaching this
compromise Constitution. The Steering Committee believes that
this allows us to continue operating in much the same manner as
we have been, only now with support and assistance from the
National AFL-CIO. It is hoped that you will take the time to go
through this and be prepared to raise questions or concerns you
may have at the October 6th General Meeting.

We hope that you too are excited about the prospect of this
affiliation. We believe that it will benefit us greatly in our
common effort to build a more active, successful and progressive
union movement.

Finally, please be sure to mail back the green delegates
form, mailed to you along with the announcement for the October
6th General Meeting. If you have misplaced it or lost it, please
just call The Labor Coalition office and leave a message or tell
one of the staff who your delegates will be.

In Solidarity,

To: The Steering Committee

RE: AFL-CIO Affiliation Process/Bylaws

March 19, 1993
To All:

Here are some thoughts on the AFL-CIO process:

You essentially have two routes to follow if the Steering Committee still
wishes AFL affiliation. These are either a)To create a parralel organization with
bylaws nearly identical to the Labor Coalition but which would be incorporated
within it; or b) to wage a fight with the AFL to have our first draft constitution
approved with whatever revisions they might require.

The first option would procede by first drafting a set of "Labor Council’
bylaws, which is essentially where the conversations with Leonard Lewis are
leading. This can probably be achieved by mid-april.

It will then be necessary to take this draft 'Labor Council’ constitution

and modify it more along the lines of the previous draft approved by the
steering committee. Here is some ideas for modifications:

a) incorporate the members of the ‘labor council’ board in its entirety to
the ‘coalition’ steering committee. Add two members for a the Labor Coalition,
and poof! you have a Steering Committee in one election at one meeting. You can
make a policy decision on matters like having only AFL unions vote on ‘Labor
Council’ members, do it all at once, etc.

b) Change the membership article to include language allowing
independants, individual members and perhaps local community organizations.

c) Names: i.e. Steering Committee vs. Executive Board, Co-Chairs vs Vice
Presidents, etc.

d) Change dues article to refer to the newly allowed organizations.

That's about it! After approving the ‘labor Council’ bylaws in their
enterity, and approving the new articles in the Labor Coalition bylaws, you may
then through the Labor Council bylaws away and only refer to the Labor
Coalition Bylaws, except in special cases as preferred by the Steering Committee
where it's deemed expedient to have only the 'Labor Council' make a decision
of some sort. It sounds more complicated than it realy is. :

The other route is to circumvent Lewis and complain to Cole and Crayton
that they are reneging on their agreements to us concerning the impact of
affiliation, and claim that our proposed original draft constitution complies with
the AFL-CIO's. This will be a fight and may become complicated and nasty, but

the steering Committee may want to pursue this route if there is concern over
the structure and cohesion of the organization.

The International Longshore and Warehouse
Union (ILWU) is engaged in a critical battle that has
implications for the entire labor movement. The —
ILWU represents 16,000 dockworkers who handle
cargo in ports along the West Coast. The union Is ne-
gotiating with the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA),
the employer group that is attempting to slash work-
ers benefits and introduce new technology aimed at
outsourcing union jobs. Companies that import -
goods through West Coast Ports, such as Payless:
ShoeSource, Wal-Mart, Home Depot, and Target have
joined together in the West Coast Waterfront Coall-
tion to support the PMA. FOR at
THE ILWU contract with the PMA expired on
July 1, 2002. In a show of good faith, the JLWU has
continued to negotiate beyond the expiration, work-
ing on a day-to-day contract extension. However, the
PMA has indicated that it may lockout ILWU members
and it is seeking federal intervention to support a
Jockout. a
The Bush Administration Is threatening the
ILWU with military action In support of a lockout of
ILWU workers in the event of an impasse In negotla-
tions. The mere threat of military Intervention Is an
unconscionable effort to bolster the boss's contract
demands and threatens legitimate bargalning rights
of longshore workers. Ona larger scale, the threat-
ened use of federal troops to determine the outcome
of a collective bargaining dispute undermines the ba-
sic civil rights of the labor movement and all Amert-

can workers. ‘
The National AFL-CIO, New York State AFL-

ClO and local labor councils are taking action by writ-
ing letters and contacting local stores that are part of
the Pacific Maritime Association in support of the
longshore workers. Midstate Central Labor Council Is
taking action by sending letters to the Bush Admint-
stration, Governor Pataki and Senators Clinton and
Schumer. Please contact the Central New York Labor
Federation for more information or if you would like

to take action.

thaca Paraprofessionals Fight for a Living Wage—
and Win!!

By Debbie Minnick, Ithaca Paraprofessionals Association

In the Fall of 2000, | had a conversation
with Carl Feuer, Health and Safety Trainer with
the Labor Coalition about the possibility of a living
wage for the members of our local— Ithaca Para-
professionals, as we started negotiating in Janu-
ary 2001. Little did | know that it would turn into
a full blown living wage campaign and continue
on until the end of June 2002!

It was probably one of the most difficult
tasks | have ever taken on but the strength,
growth and knowledge that | gained were im-
measurable. We finally settled on a 50% raise in
starting salaries by the end of the contract along
with substantial raises for everyone else.

To me this was about social issues,
women’s issues and worker's rights. The negoti-
ating team fought hard and hung in there on be-
half of 220 severely underpaid paraprofessionals
because we believed in the importance of what
they did and what they deserved.

Of course, this would not have happened
without the support that we received from the Liv-
ing Wage Coalition, NEA/NY, Midstate Central La-
bor Council, many local union members, the Labor
Religious Task Force, Alternatives Credit Union,
Cornell student groups, parents groups, |CSD stu-
dents and so many concerned citizens in the
Ithaca community. The outpouring of support was
amazing! My heartfelt thanks also goes out to all
of the paraprofessionals that hung in there
through this long, difficult process. They are true
education professionals and | will forever be hon-
ored in representing them.

The key to all of this has been community
connections and support. It has been good to go
into the summer with the contract settled. | have
enjoyed my summer and feel relaxed and re-
newed, but rest assured, if there is a group, a lo-
cal union or labor brother or sister that needs
help, | will be there for them. Just call on me!

AFL-CIO Provides Resources for Workers

Victimized by Corrupt Corporate Practices
Corporate greed has left thousands of

workers across the country without jobs, retirement
security and health care. While corporate executives
cook books and receive obscene salaries and perks,
workers are getting pink slips and losing health insur-
ance and retirement savings.

To help meet the needs of laid-off workers,
the AFL-CIO has launched www.laidoffworkers.org — a
new website that provides resources for surviving un-
employment, meeting working family challenges,
learning what went wrong and protecting retirement
security.

“Workers should not have to suffer because
of unchecked greed in corporate America,” said John
Sweeney, president of the AFL-CIO. "This new web-
site will give workers the information they need to
survive sudden layoffs in this emerging cycle of cor-
porate mismanagement."

The website, www.laidoffworkers.org, pro-
vides workers with the tools they will need to get ac-
tive in the push to demand corporate accountability.

AFL-CIO for employers facing structural change as

the announcement of Gov. Pataki's Budget Proposal

In response to the release of Governor
Pataki’s 2003-04 State Budget announcement,

made it clear that various budget cuts proposed
today may be detrimental to this state’s long term
fiscal health. He also stressed that today’s
budget announcement marks the beginning of the
discussion process to solve this crisis.

Said Hughes, “We must keep in mind that
today is only the first step in a long and hopefully
thought provoking process. While there are areas
of the Governor's budget that are very troubling to
the labor movement, we are willing to work with
Governor Pataki and both houses of the legisla-
ture to mitigate the pain that would befall those
least able to bare it.

“While we acknowledge that there are
“job killing” taxes, it should be noted that there
are also, “job killing budget cuts”. We should not
forget that certain budget cuts called for in to-
day’s proposal would potentially be devastating to
individuals and their families if job loss results.

“So we should not lose sight of the fact
that “job killing” taxes and “job killing” budget
cuts both potentially bring about the same result:
job loss and a diminished future for working fami-
lies.”

NYS AFL-CIO President Denis Hughes
stated that now is not the time for ideology to get
in the way of the monumental task at hand.

Noting that ideological baitles more often
than not favor rhetoric over common sense, Presi-
dent Hughes stated, “Action trumps ideology
every day of the week. Ideology, if not checked,
breeds intransigence. In difficult times such as
this, we cannot afford to waste a single day as we

President Hughes once again called for
shared responsibility amongst labor, business and
government as the long term solution to the crisis.

_this crisis. But sacrifice is a relative term. We are

Investing in Our Future

As a result of federal and state legislation,
Workforce Investment Boards (WI1Bs) were
formed throughout NYS about a year ago. As is-
sued by the State WIB in Albany, the mission of
these boards is “to promote economic develop-
ment through understanding the importance of
and advocating for the development and creation
ofa highly skilled workforce. Two labor repre-
sentatives, chosen by the area CLCs, serve on the
local WIBs. Fifty-one percent of the members
sitting on each WIB represent the business com-
munity.

Participation and involvement on these
Boards presents labor with opportunities but also
challenges. In order to become full and productive
partners in this system, we need to understand
the inner workings of the system. It will be neces-
sary to monitor funding and help develop pro-
grams to provide the training and education
workers need to succeed and advance in their
current jobs. We must insure that the services
and training made available to displaced workers
is adequate in preparing them for living wage and
high skill /high wage jobs. Placing these workers
in quick, dead end jobs must be discouraged by
labor. Our agenda should be focused on promot-
ing a prosperous economy through the retention
and creation of jobs that provide security for fami-
lies.

Establishing effective communication between
our unions and the WIB labor representatives
will be a critical component to our ultimate suc-
cess. Monthly Labor Council meetings will serve
as a forum for delegates to report on training
needs of its members and for the WIB labor rep-
resentatives to report on the plans and programs
of the local Board. We will share information and
discuss ways for labor’s perspective to be included

in shaping priorities, choosing training providers,
and directing funds under the WIB system.

Posting your OSHA 300 Log

Do you know where your employer's
OSHA 300 log summary is? You should know
soon, if your workplace has more than 10 em-
ployees and you are not in a low-hazard industry.
Your employer is required to post the log as of
February 1, and leave it on the bulletin board
until April 30. The log is a summary of all work-
related injuries and illnesses that occurred in
your workplace during 2002.

This will be the first time you have seen
the OSHA 300 log posted, because it has re-
placed the similar OSHA 200 log as a result of
OSHA's revision of its recordkeeping. The OSHA
300 log contains more information than the old
OSHA 200 log. By law, the information in the log
is supposed to be available for inspection by em-
ployees all year long, but the employer is only
required to display it in public for 3 months.

For more information about the OSHA
300 log and OSHA regulations concerning the
recording of work-related injuries and illnesses,
including a list of industries that are exempt
from the annual posting requirement, visit:
http://www.osha.gov/recordkeeping/index.html
If you work in the public sector in NY State, the
form to be posted is DOSH 900.1.

Just the Economic Facts

Reprinted from America at Work

JOBS
Between January 2001 and January 2003, the
nation lost a net 1.6 million jobs and almost 2.3
million private-sector jobs. During that same time
period, 1.85 million manufacturing jobs disap-
peared. The number of Americans who want jobs
today but can’t find them— an unacceptable 10
million— will grow even larger, according to Eco-
nomic Policy Institute economist Lawrence Mis-
hel. The Bush proposal will do very little to ex-
pand jobs in 2003, Mishel says, and will actually
cause the country to lose 750,000 jobs over the
next 10 years.

HEALTH CARE
After the number of uninsured declined in 1999
and 2000, it climbed to 41.2 million in 2001, ac-
cording to the U.S. Census Bureau. Of that 41.2
million, nearly 33 million were from working fami-
lies and 8.5 million were children. Workers who
still have job-based health insurance are in dan-
ger of finding it unaffordable as employers in-
creasingly shift the growing costs of coverage to
workers— between the spring of 2001 and the
spring of 2002, a single worker paid an average
27 percent more toward premiums and a family
paid an average 16 percent more than the previ-
ous year.

The continually increasing cost of pre-
scription drugs has created a crisis for retirees,
most acutely for those who work in manufacturing
where the number of retirees is growing and the
number of active workers is shrinking. Congress
must pass a Medicare drug benefit that does not
force seniors to give up their trusted doctors to
get decent drug coverage as the Bush administra-

tion ahs proposed, and does not penalize workers
whose employers offer benefits.
RETIREMENT SECURITY
Because of corporate wrongdoing, the bust of the
high-tech bubble and the recession, American stock
markets lost approximately $6.6 trillion, or about 40
percent of their value, between the market peak in
March 2000 and January 31, 2003. Such stunning
losses call for corporate governance reform, strength-
ened government oversight and the protection of So-
cial Security. According to the U.S. Social Security
Administration, Social Security was the only source of
income for 18 percent of individuals and married
couples with at least one spouse 65 or older in 2000.
The Bush administration likely will borrow a minimum
of $1.5 trillion from the Social Security Trust Fund
before Bush’s 2001 tax cuts begin to expire in 2010,
according to the Congressional Budget Office— with-
out setting aside a single penny to strengthen and
protect Social Security.
EDUCATION
At a time when states are facing budget crises and
their education funding is at risk, President George
W. Bush's 2004 fiscal year budget proposal for
schools increases their problems by failing to keep
pace with inflation and population growth. When all
programs under the federal No Child Left Behind Act
are added together, Bush’s budget provides $9 bil-
lion less than Congress authorizes for 2004 and
$199 million less than the amount needed to main-
tain purchasing power at the 2002 level, according to
the AFT. While showering tax cuts on the rich, Bush's
budget proposes eliminating after-school programs
for 500,000 children.
TRADE
Unfair trade deals such as the North American Free
Trade Agreement (NAFTA) are a central reason for the
explosion of the U.S. trade deficit. According to the
AFL-CIO Industrial Union Council, rising trade deficits
have cost 3 million actual and potential U.S. jobs
since 1994. To maintain a domestic manufacturing
base that ensures national security, the United States
must address flawed trade policies that encourage
US manufacturers to scour the globe for the lowest
wages, the weakest labor laws and the most vulner-
able workers, and oppose new trade agreements that
harm the interests of America’s workers.

est in decades, with two-thirds of adults saying
they approve of unions— a level not seen since
41967, according to a recent poll for the AFL-CiO
by Peter D. Hart Associates. Among non-union
workers who aren't managers, 47 percent say
they would vote for a union in their workplace, up
from 42 percent in January 2001.

But in the face of this growing support, it
is also clear that the public has little knowledge of
employers’ aggressive attacks against workers
trying to exercise their freedom to form unions.
More than 75 percent of those surveyed say em-
ployers should take no position when workers
want to hold a union election, but only 44 percent
say they think employers oppose workers’ effort
to join unions.

In reality, nearly all employers use unfair
tactics to oppose workers’ freedom to form un-
ions, according to Kate Bronfenbrenner. The pub-
lic strongly disapproves of employer tactics to in-
timidate workers, such as requiring supervisors to
urge employees to vote against the union and
holding mandatory, closed-door anti-union meet-
ings— but even union members far underestimate
how often employers deploy these unscrupulous
methods. For example, only 20 percent of union
members surveyed thought employers require
workers to attend anti-union meetings, which they
do 92 percent of the time.

In February, the AFL-CIO Executive Council
passed a resolution to “educate, engage and mo-
bilize literally millions of union members and peo-
ple of conscience” to expose employers’ cam-
paign against workers and support state and local
legislation that supports organizing.

TUESDAY AUGUST 5, 1986
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Now that the N.L.R.B. has ruled against the striking Cargill miners, their

Fight has entered a new stage. Union and community support has now become even
more crucial to the miners' fight for their jobs and a fair contract.

Discussions with deputies and correspondence with Sheriff Howard, have clarified

supporters rights to picket at the Lansing mine. Solidarity picketing will continue
every Tuesday from 2-4pm in Lansing.

Moosewood restaurant has announced that it will donate food every Tuesday,
and a fundraising brunch at Moosewood is in the planning stages. Painters Local
#178 has recently donated food baskets to the striking miners' families as well.
Ed Ritchie, Business Agent for the Painters Union which has brought one hundered
dollars worth of food to the miners, vowed his continued support.

Additional information has been provided to the Ithaca City Attorney
regarding Cargill's record of irresponsible corporate behavior. As further
evidence of Cargill's misconduct becomes known, we hope to see Ithaca and other
cities re-evaluate their business relationship with Cargill Salt for the duration
of the strike.

One hundred miners are still on strike, and more than ever in need of support

from their neighbors and from our community. If you can help in any way, please
contact the Labor Coalition at 272-4108 or attend a Miners Solidarity Meeting, Monday

evenings at 7:30pm, 109 W. State.

A little conquest in Lansing

Cargill, Inc., a multinational empire,
seeks free rein in the local salt mine

to gain complete power to determine who works in
what job and for how long, for how much pay and for
what benefits, and with what hazards to life and
health. In short, they want to get free rein in the
workplace by consolidating their control over the

lives of the workers.

What Cargill is really “offering”
The terrns of management's offer indicate Car-

gill's aims clearly. Wages are not the issue: Cargill
has already agreed to a wage increase. The major
sticking points are four Cargill proposals that, taken
as a package, would render the workers powerless
even if the union were somehow to survive,

It is important to look at the proposals in detail,
since newspaper accounts that describe the dispute as
“involving issues of seniority” can make it sound as
though Cargill is simply trying to rescue the career
opportunities of newer workers from the entrenched
privileges of older workers. As such, busting the
union might seem like a favor to the workforce, since
Cargill would be replacing a policy of “protecting the
dead wood” with a system of rewards by merit. In
this way, superficial reporting can serve as
propaganda for the cause of the Cargill empire.

One part of Cargill's package involves the way
new job openings are to be filled. At first glance, the
proposal seems like it would fulfill the American
dream of advancement according to merit. Bids for
jobs would be judged according to the skills that the
bidders possess. If no single bidder excelled the
others by this criterion, Cargill would use the
criterion of “overall ability to perform the job.”
Finally, if these criteria produced no winner, Cargill
would look for the most senior bidder among those
bidders who are currently employed in the mine.

By comparison, the current system, which ranks
seniority first in consideration, skills second, and

in fixed assets like buildings and machinery: Cargill
deals with cash, and lots of it. As a result, the
company finds it easy to move its assets around, and
this means that Cargill can afford to pour money into
operations that are losing money temporarily—as the
Lansing mine may be doing right now. Thus,
Cargill, as a trading company, resembles a big bank
as much as it resembles a big manufacturing
company: to lay out a large amount of cash (to buy a
million tons of wheat, or to survive a strike) in order
to reap a huge profit later (by selling the wheat abroad
when prices go up, or by busting the mineworkers'
union) is Cargill's standard business practice, and the
company is specially set up to operate this way.

Cargill's other money advantage comes from
being privately owned. As such, the MacMillan and
Cargill families do not have to attract stockholders by
paying large dividends. In fact, families controlling
such empires tend to shelter themselves from taxes by
undervaluing their assets and paying themselves low
dividends. The extra money is reinvested in the
company, and in the case of Cargill, the capital is
reserved as cash for contingencies like a sweet
purchase of soybeans—or for weathering a strike.

There is another advantage to being privately
owned: secrecy. Cargill is not required to publish
detailed figures on any of its operations. In fact,
when the mineworkers' negotiating committee asked
to inspect the books that Cargill keeps for the mine
(a standard practice to insure that a company is really
in the shape it claims to be in), Cargill refused. The
Cargills and MacMillans lead very private lives, after
all, and the world's largest grain traders are not
accountable to anyone.

bers are Reagan appointees. The point of law in
question is whether the strike is motivated by the mi-
ners’ economic demands or whether it is a response to
Unfair Labor Practices (ULP’s). If the strike is de-
clared economic, Cargill is not obliged to re-hire any
strikers, but if it is judged a ULP strike, Cargill must

take everyone back. (When Cargill offered to take
back the 47 miners, it also demanded that the ULP
cases be dropped. Cargill was asking a minority of
the strikers to sell out the jobs of the majority.)

The union has already won a ULP case charging
Cargill with bad-faith bargaining; Cargill cancelled
out on six negotiating sessions and then sprang its
“offer” on the union just a few days before the last
contract expired. The regional NLRB told Cargill to
behave better in the future. The Reagan-appointed
national board is to decide whether this ULP, plus
another charge of bad-faith bargaining (Cargill
negotiators held up the start of a bargaining session
until 2 a.m.), substantiate the union's claim that this
is a “ULP strike.” A victory at the NLRB would not
settle the strike in the union's favor, but it would
assure the mineworkers that they won't lose their jobs
permanently while bargaining coritinues.

Why others should join the fight:
the imperatives of solidarity

Members of the community, of course, have a
morai obigaiion to help out their neighbors in ime

f need, but there are imperatives of seli-intercsi, too.
The dispute is not an isolated disagreement between 2
company and a few workers; its outcome will have
effects on similar struggles elsewhere. Labor defeats
in a few local industries can depress wages and affect
employment patterns throughout the area. We stress
again that the miners’ struggle is a political struggle
for power over their lives, and it is part of a broader
local and national struggle in which a wealthy
minority has the upper hand against the majority.
The front line of this struggle is often the picket line,
and we know from experience that broad-based
support for those at the front line can turn the tide.
In this area, the front line is now in Lansing.

To join the struggle, contact the Cargill Strikers’
Solidarity Committee (CSSC), care of the Tompkins-
Cortland Labor Coalition, 109 W. State Street,
Ithaca, NY 14850 (phone 607-272-4108). CSSC
meets Mondays at 7:30 p.m. in the Labor Coalition's
office above the State Theater.

Dear Matt:

The Labor Coalition had a terrific rally in support of the Cargill miners
this past Saturday. Numerous local labor leaders, Democratic leaders, and church
folk spoke in support of the miners' cause. We even got favorable coverage in the
Journal so you KNOW it must have been good!

I wanted to thank you on behalf of the Labor Coalition for your letter of
interest which was read at the rally. I am aware of the awkwardness such struggles
cause for you, not to mention one which is taking place outside your district.
However, just as the Reagan administration has effectively dismantled other

fundamental systems of justice and due process in our society, so hath they wrought
with our labor laws. I believe it is incumbent on community leaders to help restore

some semblance of balance and fair play. Your interest has helped in that regard.
Thanks again, I look forward to discussing these kinds of concerns with you in
the coming months.

Very truly,

Al Davidoff

i May 17, 1986

Dear Friends:

I am very concerned about the situation at Cargill. A
he long record of labor-management cooperation has come to an
aan” abrupt end with this dispute, which is now in its eighth week.
a As I understand it, the union workers, members of the Machinists
Union, are asking for a renewal of their recently expired
contract; Cargill has begun to bring in permanent replacements

for the striking workers; and the National Labor Relations Board
has said that Cargill should be bargaining in good faith.

This country has a long and proud history of workers
struggling for better working conditions and decent wages. That
struggle was not in vain, for it finally produced a generally C
constructive relationship between labor and management, one in BS
which good faith bargaining has usually generated better
economic conditions for both parties and for our communities. h

But good faith bargaining is crucial to this process and
the progress which has resulted. In this case, both parties
should return to the table and negotiate. Let the bargaining
be hard, let the negotiations be vigorous, but let them proceed --
openly and without bitterness. An agreement, fairly arrived at,
would be in the interest of all parties and this community.

Thank you.
Sincerely,
Matthew F. McHugh

operated as a not-for-profit organization to support local member unions through educational and informational

programs. Membership in the Labor Council is open to affiliated local unions, councils, joint boards, district
councils, and other organizations supporting the goals of the Labor Council.

Basis of Accounting

The Labor Council's policy is to prepare its financial statements on the cash basis of accounting;
consequently, revenues are recognized when received rather than when earned, and expenses are
recognized when cash is disbursed rather than when the obligation is incurred.

Fund Accounting

To ensure observance of limitations and restrictions placed on the use of resources available to the Labor
Council, the accounts of the Council are maintained in accordance with the principles of fund accounting. That

is the procedure by which resources for various purposes are classified for accounting and reporting purposes

into funds established according to their nature and purposes. Separate accounts are maintained for each
fund.

The assets, liabilities, and net assets of the Council are reported in three self-balancing fund groups as
follows:

The General Fund, also known as the Operating Fund, represents the portion of expendable funds that are
available for support of the various unions.

The Health & Safety Fund accounts for the New York State Department of Labor Grant.

The Cortland Area Workers Rights Fund is a spin-off organization supporting union workers in Cortland
County.

In planning and performing our audit of the financial statements of the Mid-State Central Labor Council for the
year ended December 31, 1998, we considered the internal control structure to determine our auditing
procedures for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the financial statements and not to provide
assurance on the internal control structure.

However, during our audit, we became aware of matters that are an opportunity for strengthening operating
efficiencies. This letter summarizes our current year comments and recommendations regarding these
matters. This letter does not affect our report dated February 25, 1999.

CURRENT FINDINGS:

Payment of Invoices

: : Zz Finding:

= During our current year audit, we noted that the system of authorization for invoices was not being used for
all invoices. Payroll for hourly employees was not consistently authorized by the supervisor. Payments for
payroll were sometimes combined with expense reimbursements.

Recommendation:

We recommend that all payments of invoices and hourly payroll for employees be authorized and invoices
should be stamped with the check number and date of payment to indicate that they have been paid. All
reimbursement of expenses for employees should be done with a separate check.

Interfund Transactions

a Finding:
Bie During our current year audit, we noted that there were a number of invoices being paid from the General
Fund for the Health and Safety Fund (H&S) and visa-versa.

Efe Recommendation:
Bos While it is not a requirement of the DOL contract, we recommend that only invoices that are split between the

x two funds be paid from the other fund. Otherwise, all H&S invoices should be paid from the H&S checking
Eas) account and all General Fund expenses be paid from the General Fund. If H&S does not have sufficient
ws money to pay their bills the General Fund can lend them money. The loans/advances between the funds

It should be noted that procedures have been put into place in 1999 to allow the monthly reconciliation of the

Dues Receivable

Finding:
During our current year audit, we noted that the treasurer did not have sufficient information to know if all of
the per capita dues had been collected for the year.

Recommendation:

We recommend that a system be set up for the treasurer to know what dues have been paid and what dues
are still outstanding.

Organizational Identity

Finding:

During our current year audit, we noted that the identity of the Organization is not consistently stated. The old
Organization is The Tompkins Cortland Labor Coalition, Inc., the new Organization is the Mid-State Central
Labor Council. Each Organization has their own federal identification number.

Recommendation:

We recommend that all bank accounts, payroll tax filings, income tax filings and contracts be in the name of
the Mid-State Central Labor Council and that the federal identification number being used should be the
number for the Labor Council. We recommend that if the Labor Council wants to use the Labor Coalition
name that they should file a doing business as form with the Tompkins County Clerk to make it clear that the
Organization is the Labor Council. If the Labor Council no longer wants to use the Labor Coalition name then
they should notify the Secretary of State that they want to dissolve the corporation.

We will review the status of these comments during our next audit engagement. We have already discussed
these comments and suggestions with the Council personnel, and will be pleased to discuss them in further
detail at your convenience, to perform any additional study of these matters, or to assist you in implementing
the recommendations.

This letter is intended for the information of the management of the Mid-State Central Labor Council and its

Newfield Teachers Out On The Line

The Newfield Teachers’
Association (NTA) is standing
Strong in their struggle for a more
equitable contract with the New-
field School Board. After 17
months of working without a con-
tract, some progress has been
made but the School Board has
still not come up with a proposal
that addresses the major inequities
in the compensations system.

The teachers’ salaries in
the Newfield School District lag
far behind the salaries of other
Tompkins County teachers. In
fact, not only is the Newfield

teachers’ median salary the lowest
for any public school in Tompkins
County, it is ranked 574th out of
597 districts in New York State.
The District’s present
salary proposal is still just over 3%
in the next two years, lower than
the salary increases received by

other teachers in the County. At
this rate, the District will continue
to lose some of its best teachers to
districts that are willing to pay

“Our salaries are already
considered lower and to
take that kind of hit just
puts people further be-
hind.”

more competitive salaries and to
reward teachers for loyalty and
length of service. As of now,
eight experienced teachers have
resigned this year.

Meanwhile, the District is
also proposing givebacks on
health insurance, with higher pre-
mium rates, and a bigger percent-
age paid by the teachers. For new
employees, the situation is partic-
ularly bad. According to the Dis-

trict’s present proposal new em-
ployees would get a $1,000.00 pay
increase with $1400.00 givebacks
on health insurance. “That’s just
unacceptable,” says Albert Com-
fort, President of the Teachers’
Association. “Our salaries are al-
ready considered lower and to take
that kind of hit just puts people
further behind.”

The Union has met with the
District and a federal mediator in
recent weeks and made progress
on some non-economic issues.

The Newfield Teachers’ As-
sociation was joined by other local
labor activists at an information
picket in front of Newfield Schools
on November 29 and November 6.

education aimed at increasing understanding of

in behalf of Cayuga Medical Center Nurses Association/CSEA

LABOR ALERT

A group of Registered Nurses at the Cayuga Medical Center have recently decided to
organize a union with the help of CSEA/AFSCME, Local 1000.

Important issues in the nurses’ organizing campaign are:
|. Inadequate staffing, with units often working short staffed

2. Heavy demands placed on nurses to work extra-long shifts, and to work extra shifts on short
notice

3. Assignment of nursing duties to unqualified and untrained hospital staff
4. Cayuga Medical Center’s lack of commitment to continuing education for it’s nursing staff

These issues are important to the nurses at Cayuga Medical Center. These issues are
also vital to the quality of health care available to the residents of Tompkins County!

Nurses Need Your Help!

Cayuga Medical Center management was asked by CSEA to subscribe to a set of
principles (“Principles of a Fair Campaign”) which would guarantee an organizing campaign free
of intimidation and threats. These principles include an atmosphere of mutual respect between
the hospital and union; a commitment by the hospital to refrain from “captive audience”

meetings and “one-on-one” supervisor to employee mectings; and no discharges, disciplinary
actions, and no transfers of nurses to isolated work areas or shifts, duc to union activity.

Cayuga Medical Center has made it clear that it has no intention of subscribing to
the “Principles of a Fair Campaign”. Nurses will thus, need every bit of support the Labor

Movement and Community Organizations have to offer. Below, we have listed two tasks
we would ask supporters of a nurses’ union to do. These are:

1. Write a letter to Bonnie Howell, President and CEO of Cayuya Medical Center. This letter
should state your support for a Nurses’ Union, and should call on the hospital to subscribe to
the “Principles of a Fair Campaign”. A sample letter is included on the back of this Alert.

2. If you are a union member, or, if you are part of an organization Which would support nurses’

efforts to form a union, we would like to be invited to your next mecting to talk about the issues
and how you and your organization/union can help.

When the Dryden Sertoma Soccer teams kick the first ball this September, they will
know if it's a Foulball. Several hundred children will receive soccer balls at the start of
the season and Sertoma has made every effort to assure that these were not made with
child labor. It is not an easy road, but one which follows the lead of the Federation
Internationale de Football Associations, better known to us as the International Soccer
League. After video footage revealed children sewing soccer balls with the World Cup
Logo and Pele signature, FIFA declared that the 1998 World Cup would be
childlabor-free. Did they achieve their goal? 70% of all soccer balls are made in one
Pakistani town, Sialkot. The Foulball Campaign, developed to monitor and encourage all
soccer leagues to use discretion in purchasing equipment, is the most recent effort in a
90-year global history.

In 1919 the International Labor Organization was formed following World War I and the
Bolshevik Revolution, in an effort to prevent future worker unrest. To date there have
been 178 Conventions, 11 of which the US has signed. Within the original charter was a
definition of child labor as work done by anyone under the age of 14. It was also at the
tur of the century that the US was eliminating child labor (and we are still trying). The
ILO Convention #138 broadened its child labor restriction in 1973 such that children
should not work until the legal age for completion of school. The US did not sign. After
World War II, the International Trade Organization and eventually GATT were designed

to promote "free trade."

The Shah of Iran declared in 1975 that child labor would be outlawed in his country's
carpet industry. Prime Minister Indira Ghandi saw this as a windfall for India and opened
many new carpet factories, bringing in lower caste children, who were considered
uneducable and dispensable, to serve as laborers. This was not out of character with the
prevailing view that "if we educate them they won't want to work in our fields."
(UNICEF 1997 State of the World's Children) By 1980 there had begun a crusade to
release children from bonded labor and servitude. In 1985 a Grenada film showed the
world conditions of children working and got the attention of London Markets. The
Western countries began to take notice and backed by German markets, the South Asian
Coalition on Child Servitude (SACCS) initiated what was to become the Rugmark
Campaign. By 1994 there was a monitoring process and labeling method. Most

important for Rugmark was its Education Fund.

In the United States some few people were taking notice. The Pease-Harkin Bill, which
eventually Senator Tom Harking (D-Iowa) rewrote, began in 1990. In reaction to the
exposure of American markets importing goods made with child labor, thousands of
children were put out on the streets. Looking for other work, they turned to more
dangerous jobs, such as recovering lead from spent batteries with bare hands and feet,
and an expansion of the sex trade. This tragedy led to efforts not only to prohibit
children from bonded labor and exploitation, but also to get them into school and

9/16/88 10-06 AM
Stephens

provide them with a small stipend. The Harkin Bill finally passed in 1997 along with the
Sanders Amendment to the Tariff Act of 1930. So why do we know nothing of this, and
why do we have no way of knowing if the malls are filled with items made by children?
Because our commitment to Gatt precludes us from "imposing social sanctions, which
would be seen as technical barriers to free trade." Would we, the leader of capitalist free
trade, want to deter the lowest sectors of other economies from earning a "living?" There
is another way to pose the question: What do we need so badly that a child should
sacrifice his childhood or her education? This presentation was given to the Dryden
Sertoma Club on September 3, 1998.

Labor Activists...."A moder political miracle, the defeat of Califomia Propo-
sition 226 by an overall 54 to 46% margin, sprang from the voters strong
sense of fairness and union members’ unprecedented mobilization against
a right-wing effort to silence the voices of working men and women in our
nation’s political system. Union members rejected the proposition with a

Union Leader Takes New Position

Al Davidoff, President of UAW Local 2300 and Co-chair
ef the Labor Coalition, today announced that as of Monday
March 31 he will be leaving these positions to become the
AFL-CIO’s Director for New York State.

Davidoff attended the ILR School at Cormeld from 1976-
1980 during which time he began working full-time as a
custodian. He became active in the effort to organize among
Cornell workers which culminated in the successful union

vote in 1981 that created Local 2300.

Davidoff was elected the first President of UAW 2300 in
1982. In 1984, he was instrumental in the founding of the
Labor Coalition, bringing together 40 unions from the Ithaca

and Cortland area and has served as that organization’s
Chair since then.

Over the past decade, Davidoff helped over a dozen

other workplaces unionize, including HOMES, Video Ithaca,
the Holiday Inn, and the Public Library.

Davidoff is perhaps best known for forcefully bringing
local labor struggles into the public realm in campaigns

like the
University.

CIO’s top position for New York State, the nation’s most
heavily unionized state with almost 2 million members. In
his new role, Davidoff will be a key player in the AFL-CIO’s
new aggressive campaign to mobilize the Labor movement
around organizing, rank-and-file activism, political action

and the fight for all working families in our communities.
He will remain an Ithaca resident.

The TEAM Act is dangerous because it would
allow employers to hand-pick who would represent
workers on "employee committees" that deal with

workers and what subjects could be discussed. It
would also give unscrupulous employers a powerful
tool to undermine organizing drives. In effect it

would legalize the establishment of company un-
ions.

principles of our labor law - that workers should
have the right to self-determination by democrati-

Cally electing their own independent representa-
tives.

Science has discovered
the ability to clone sheep.

Now Big Business wants to
‘clone’ itself into company unions, and
the anti-worker forces in Congress
want to let them do it!

SWE have now discovered how to clone an identical sheep from an existing one. Many people
are talking about its potential future effects. For American workers, however, a different type of

“cloning” is being pushed by Big Business and the anti-union forces in Congress. It would have
disastrous effects on workers’ ability to have an independent voice in the workplace.

The U.S. Senate is set to vote this week on legislation known as the TEAM Act (S.295). Under this
bill, management would be given the right to dominate and interfere with employee involvement
programs, or “teams.” Under S. 295, management would be allowed to create and disband worker
committees, handpick the committee members (“cloning” management's viewpoint), dictate the
agenda, and even determine the outcome of any decisions made by the committee.

In short, S.295 would give Big Business the ability to establish “company unions!’ The AFL-CIO and
its affiliated unions are strongly opposed to this legislation.

Union members nationwide are being asked to call their U.S. Senators immediately to urge them to
vote NO on this bill when it comes up for a vote.

Simply call the AFL-CIO toll-free action hotline at 1-800-LABOR-21
(1-800-522-6721) and ask to speak to Senator Alfonse D’Amato.
Tell him to vote NO on S. 295.

UNION CITIES

Equal Strong Communities

Strong, vibrant unions make Amencan cities and towns better places to live and
work. To help bning €conomuc security and justice to working families and a healthier
political and social environment to the community as a whole, the AFL-CIO Union Cities

program will provide a framework through Central Labor Councils to rebuild the labor
movement at its grassroots. }

Central Labor Councils will be challenged to bring local unions together around a
set of eight goals designed to build stronger unions, stronger labor councils and stronger -
communities, and then pass a resolution committing themselves to meet these goals.

Central Labor Councils that have committed to become Union Cities will be
announced in early 1997, and councils whose jurisdictions achieve Union City status will

be recognized annually thereafter.

The Union Cities resolution commits the CLC and its local unions to work toward
the following goals:

e Enrolling at least half of the local unions in the CLC in the AFL-CIO “Changing to
Organize” program, which guides local unions in coordination with their
international unions toward shifting at least 30 percent of their resources into
organizing, and adopting and implementing an organizing plan;

Recruiting and activating at least one percent of the total union membership in the
jurisdiction as part of a rapid response/solidarity team that can be mobilized to

support worker struggles in the community;

Reaching an overall membership growth rate in the jurisdiction of three percent
per year by the year 2000;

a Organizing grassroots legislatve/political action committees from the precinct
level up, with at least 100 union activists in each local and legislative district in the
council’s jurisdiction, and mobilizing members as well as community parmers;

SI Sponsoring the new AFL-CIO economucs education program for a majority of the
local unions in the jurisdiction;
| Building public support for the nght of workers to join unions by successfully
sponsoring a city council resolution supporting the right to organize and by
insisting that candidates for local, state and federal office pledge to use their public
stature to support organizing as a condition of political endorsement;

a Ensunng that the entre smmucture of the local labor councils -- from the Executive

Board to the delegate body -- reflects the face of the community in which we
intend to mobilize and organize;

& Working with community allies on economic development strategies that establish
community standards for local industnies and public investment.

Central Labor Councils will work with their state field directors to develop and
implement action plans. CLCs seeking Union City status will be evaluated on their
progress toward reaching these goals, not on absolute accomplishment. Union Cities will

be prionity cities for AFL-CIO programming (such as America Needs A Raise town
meetings and Union Summer).

The Union Cities program represents a fundamental change in the roles and
Tesponsibilities of the AFL-CIO’s Central Labor Councils. It is a long-term challenge to
CLCs to fulfill their mission to organize in the community to promote social and
economic justice for all working people.

Dear Brother Wynns,

I am responding to your letter of February 28, 1996 to President Sweeney which we received in the
Organizing Department on April 12, 1996.

First, let me apologize for the delay in answering you letter. The role of CLCs in organizing is of particular
interest to us as we look to help increase organizing activity and membership levels.

Your proposal is both interesting and thought provoking. I would like to share with you a few reactions to it.
But, first, I ought to make clear that under the guidelines established by the Executive Council the project you
propose would not seem to qualify. (The Organizing Fund has been designated to target large scale
organizing that involves a partnership between several International unions and the AFL-CIO. )

With that behind us, let me react to some points in your proposal.

The agenda for the training conference is interesting and probably useful. I would add a section on building
the internal capacity of unions to organize, especially using rank and file. The overall weakness of many
organizing trainings that occur is that they are not tied directly to an organizing effort. Often the participants
don’t organize, don’t have a full time organizer on staff, and don’t have a strategic plan for focusing the
organizing that they do. Your program may not have this weakness, but to the extent you can tie it to actual
organizing targets, actual plans to build organizing capacity and actual organizing campaigns, the better it
will be.

I suspect that you are in familiar with the basic message of Cornell’s Kate Bronfenbrenner studies and her
latest piece “It takes more than house calls...”. It points out the importance of using a “comprehensive”
approach in organizing and generally is consistent with points 2,3 & 4. I have found the quantitative parts of
her studies convincing to many union leaders and organizers.

The objective of recruiting and training 40-60 rank and file members and community activists to serve as
volunteer organizers, coupled with the computer matching of rank and file organizers with organizing leads
suggests that you are thinking of developing an organizing model that differs from that commonly seen. I am
interested in any further thoughts you have about this. How would it work? Is this for the 40-60 volunteer

SOUTH-CENTRAL NEW YORK

A Grant Proposal

Submitted to the AFL-CIO Organizing Institute and the Department

of Organization and Field Services, AFL-CIO

The Midstate Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO

The Midstate Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO (MCLC) is interested
in carrying out a program to increase the number of organizing
drives within our jurisdiction, and the success rate of organiz-
ing drives when they occur. We do not have the resources to
develop and implement such a jurisdiction-wide organizing pro-
gram. We are thus asking the AFL-CIO to help fund this program
with a one year grant of $20,000 for 1996.

The Program

The program we are proposing is based on a two-part strategy.
First, to increase the number of organizing leads and actual
organizing drives, we seek to implement an outreach strategy to
increase labor’s presence within the community and our contact
with unorganized workers.

Second, to increase the success rate of organizing drives, we
believe it will be necessary to develop a large cadre of union
members who can serve as volunteer, rank and file organizers and
to provide training to the officers and staff of our affiliates
around organizing strategies and tactics.

What We Propose To Do

Objective #1: Run a training conference for local union officers
and staff on organizing. The purpose of this conference is to
train and re-train local union officers and staff in running NLRB
election, PERB election, and non-NLRB election organizing drives.
Within the context of NLRB and PERB election oriented drives, the
focus will be on developing effective strategies aimed at coun-
tering and overcoming employer opposition. This training confer-
ence will also emphasize a definition of organizing which in-
cludes the attainment of a first contract.

Conference to be a full day event with training focused on; 1.)
targeting and evaluating organizing leads towards the identifi-
cation of viable organizing drives (including the attainment of a
first contract), 2.) planning and developing an organizing
strategy based on the targeting assessment, 3.) building multi-
union, cooperative organizing strategies, 4.) organizing communi-
ty-labor coalitions and effectively using community-labor coali-
tions within the context of an organizing drive.

Objective #2: Recruit and train 40-60 rank and file union
members and community activists to serve as volunteer organizers.

We will provide four full-day training programs for 10 to 15
participants each. The training will cover organizing strate-
gies, how to follow up on leads, conducting home visits and
phoning. Participants will be recruited through affiliated
unions as well as from the community. Grant funds are needed to
cover all lost time expenses for the union members, as well as
other training costs. Once trained, the grass-roots organizers
will be available for use by affiliate unions in organizing
drives.

Objective #3: Run five community-based programs on basic
workers‘ rights, targeting non-union workers. '
The two-hour programs will take place in each of the Counties
within our jurisdiction. We will conduct extensive outreach —
prior to each program, including flyers, word-of-mouth, advertiz-
ing, PSAs. and so on. Focus to be on limited statutory
protections for workers, how unorganized workers can use those
limited statutory protections/programs in their own behalf, and
the role unions play in widening workers’ rights.

Objective #4: Organize a Workers’ Rights Board in Cortland.

The Board will be made up of approximately 20 progressive-minded
professionals, trade unionists, clergy and political leaders.
Staff will review complaints received from workers, investigate
and attempt to reach a settlement with employer. The Board will
review those complaints which are valid but where the employer
takes an intractable stand. The effectiveness of Board would be
based on the use of public pressure. The existence of a WRB will
serve to greatly increase labor’s role in the community and the
number of organizing leads we receive.

Objective #5: Develop computer capability to match rank and file
organizers with unorganized workers on a geographic, private or
public sector, industry basis. Although not a difficult task,
Matching organizers with unorganized workers based on a number of
criteria will increase the effectiveness of the rank and file
organizers’s contact. While union members’ addresses and affili-
ations are easily obtainable through the New York State Federa-
tion, criteria coding will need to be accomplished locally. The
MCLC will coordinate the database and its use with the organizing
union.

Rationale
During the last two years, MCLC and our affiliates have experi-
enced a substantial increase in the number of contacts from
unorganized workers interested in forming a union at their
workplace. During 1995:

The MCLC received two organizing leads in Cortland, one from
workers at a sheltered workshop and involved a potential
bargaining unit of 75 workers, and the second from workers
at the Marietta Corporation, a potential bargaining unit of
approximately 300 warehouse and production workers. Both
leads led to short-lived organizing drives by UAW Local 2300
assisted by MCLC. Neither drive leading to a representation
election.

There were two organizing drives in the Ithaca area. A
drive at the Therm Corporation involving a potential bar-

gaining unit of 300 production workers was aborted when not
enough workers signed cards. A drive at the DAKA Corpora-
tion, a food service contractor at Ithaca College, was, lost

when the union was defeated in a 41 to 30 vote. Both drives
were led by UAW Local 2300.

SEIU Local 200B is currently involved in a drive to organize
part-time faculty members employed by BOCES, an continuing
ed./vocational training center. 200B is also involved in
organizing approximately 120 dietary, building and grounds,
group home counseling and vocational counseling employees at

George Jr. Republic, a New York State sub-contracted facili-
ty for court placed adolescents.

SEIU Local 200A recently won an election at the Tioga Carsy:
Hospital in Corning, New York where over 500 service and
Maintenance workers and RNs voted to unionize.

During 1995 we also received about 350 information and |
referral calls from area workers, a large number of which

were from unorganized workers, many in distress, each one a
potential organizing lead.

Our 1995 record, while showing an increase in organizing activi-
ty, did not lead to organizing successes. The reasons for our
lack of success are fairly clear and easily understood.

First, in all cases, these private sector employers responded to
the organizing drive with very stiff opposition. Through the use
of "traditional" employer tactics, these employers were able to

isolate workers, deliver the usual management distortions in one-

on-one and captive audience meetings, and overpower any message
or counter-message from the union.

The union and the MCLC were unable to muster the necessary re-
sources in order to Overpower the employer’s tactics. In virtu-
ally all cases, the union and MCLC were not able to activate
enough union members or build a strong enough public presence
necessary in order to gain and hold the momentum in these drives.

Our goal, therefore, and the focus of the organizing program
contained in this proposal, is to increase our organizing re-
sources. We propose a two part strategy based on a "labor

movement" approach to organizing rather than an approach which

pits unorganized workers and the union against the employer
single-handedly.

First, we will increase our contact with unorganized workers and
strengthen our presence in the community through the "workers’

rights" education sessions and through the formation of a Workers
Rights Board in Cortland.

Second, will increase our organizing success rate by having a
corps of grass-roots organizers available, by making greater use
of computer technology and also by the community out-
reach/presence mentioned above.

Why We Are the One’s To Do It

The Midstate Central Labor Council has a long history as an
activist labor council. Founded in 1982, the MCLC has been
active in supporting its affiliates through strike support, has
worked with its affiliates in developing inside contract cam-
paigns and coordinating union-community campaigns around job loss
and plant closing issues. Many of these MCLC campaigns include,
and are run by activists from many different unions. Thus, MCLC

activities are perceived by the community as "labor" activities
in the widest sense of the word.

Some of the campaigns the MCLC has been involved in are as
follows:

1. In 1994 the MCLC with APWU, Local 1151 and the UAW, Local
2300, led a campaign to stop the formation of a mail consor-
tium between the USPS, Cornell University and Ithaca Col-
lege. This mail consortium would have led to the elimina-

tion of up to forty regular postal jobs with regular postal
workers being replaced by sheltered workshop workers. This
Campaign also included a strong community based component.

2. In 1993, the MCLC organized strike support including
volunteer picketing for Borg-Warner workers represented by
Machinists, Local Lodge 1607. In 1994, IAM, Local Lodge
1607 and the MCLC ran a community campaign around plant

closings when NCR announced the sale of its Ithaca located
manufacturing and research facility.

3. In 1993, the MCLC and a number of Cortland, New York
based unions including UAW, Local 1326; UAW, Local 802;
CSEA, Local 605; and NYSUT, Local 2190 (United University
Professors) led a community campaign against the Smith-
Corona Corp. after Smith-Corona announce the layoff of over
800 of its Cortland workers. Smith-Corona workers were and
are unorganized; This campaign focused on Smith Corona’s

irresponsible corporate behavior to the community , includ-
ing many WARN Act violations.

4, In 1992-93, the MCLG) in conjunction with CSEA, Local 428
and PEF Local 251 organized a community based campaign to
keep the state-run Willard Psychiatric Center open after
being slated for shutdown. This campaign involved extensive

political organizing and the organization of a couple
community-labor rallies.

5. In 1991-92, the MCLC organized support for Teamsters,
Local 317, in their organizing campaign with the Ithaca, NY
A aanetnnen Dndaentino af Tahar and Caonorecc of Inductrial Oroanizatione

based American Community Cablevision (ACC). This campaign
involved MCLC activists in working directly with engineering

and office workers at ACC and building support rallies in
behalf of organizing workers. The MCLC carried its support

of the ACC workers through the organizing drive and the
achievement of a first contract.

6. The MCLC worked with the Ithaca Teachers Association and
Ithaca Paraprofessional Association towards the achievement
of these unions’ first decent contracts. The MCLC was
primarily involved in building community support.

The MCLC has also worked with area construction trades unions on
the adaptation of a county residency requirement for public

building projects and establishing pre-hire agreements between Ee
building trades unions and the City of Ithaca, New York. iy

In addition to the above, the MCLC runs an occupational health
and safety program which includes publishing a health and safety
newsletter, FYI, provides occupational health and safety training
to organized and unorganized workers in the area, consults with
affiliated unions on occupational health and safety issues, and ie
functions as an area wide health and safety advocacy program pe
directly working with impacted workers. The MCLC’s health and
safety program is funded through a grant with the New York
Department of Labor.

The MCLC is also involved in running a new Union Leadership
Development Program in conjunction with the Cornell University
Industrial and Labor Relations Extension Program and has run
trainings independently as well. Finally, the MCLC publishes a

bi-monthly newspaper, The Working Press.

The above is meant to highlight the central role played by the
MCLC in its jurisdiction. Many functions outside of the direct
representation of organized workers occur through the MCLC, and,
as a result, the MCLC has established a legitimacy, both inside
and outside the labor movement as the voice of the labor movement ve
in the area. Based on this legitimacy and the central role oe)
played by the MCLC in labor matters in this area, the MCLC is oa
really, the only organization capable of leading and coordinating
an area wide organizing program.

DIRECTIONS COMITTEE:
Meeting of April 10, 1996

Present: Gerry Evans, UAW #1326; John Gillis, Carpenters #603; Mark
Keith, UAW #802; Ron Powell, UAW #802; Len Usefara,
Carpenters #603: Chuck Wynns, MCLC; Mark Reader, SEIU

Not Present: Tom Joyce, Painter #178

I. Working Press

a. Committee members all stated that the Working Press is a key
MCLC project which should continue. The regularity of the
paper has been a problem and efforts should be directed
towards making the paper timely. Chuck W. did let committee
members know about a Working Press brainstorming meeting on

May 1 or 2 aimed towards a full re-thinking of the Working
Press.

b. Directions Committee members made a number of

reccomendations on the Working Press; these reccomendations
are:

-If the WP continues on a once every two months basis, we
should try a topical, rather than a news approach. For
instance, an October edition might be built around the
subject of local and regional elections. Other editions
might include topics such as "bargaining health care",
"innovative organizing strategies", "health care reform",

"Labor political strategies", "occupational health and
safety",etc.

-Another idea discussed was to purchase a page or two in the
Cortland Standard, Ithaca Journal, or, more realistically,
the Pennysaver, for the purpose of announcing events,

reporting local labor news items, etc. A Pennysaver based
approach has the following advantages:

1.lots of people receive the Pennnysaver

2.could be released on a frequent basis

II. General Meetings

Most folks present felt that General Meetings have not been well
attended, seem to lack excitement, and thus, have not been
very successful. Because the Labor Coalition holds only three
general meetings per year, there is no sense as to how delegates
can play a meaningful role in Labor Coalition business.
Additionally, a number of Directions Committee members felt that
holding three meetings per year tended to reinforce a perception
that General Meetings are not important which, in turn,
reinforces a perception that the Labor Coalition is not
important. Thus, Directions Committee members reccommend
increasing the number of General Meetings to six per year on a
once every two months basis. Ideas for improving attendance at
General meetings are as follows:

-Make the meetings more interesting. Every General Meeting
should feature a speaker and include a discussion around the
speaker’s topic. Speakers and topics should be interesting,
provocative, and educational. We should "advertise" our
General Meetings based on the speaker/topic; for instance,
given proper notice, Len stated he would be able to announce

upcoming General Meeting topics in the Carpenters’
newsletter.

-Bring politicians in to speak at general Meetings. Format,
for instance, would be to let the politician speak for 10
Minutes, then 20 minutes of question and answer. Such a
format, members felt, would be fun, increase delegates’
understanding of the political process, and reinforce
labor’s impact on the political front.

TII. Constitutional Amendment

A definite trend in the Labor Coalition’s history has been a
tendency towards devisiveness, in some cases leading to
affiliated local unions leaving the Coalition. Recent examples
include a resolution on the Gulf War and a resolution supporting
the City of Ithaca’s withholding of building permits.

A key factor leading to the devisiveness tendency is the central
role of the Steering Committee in defining and approving Labor
Coalition public positions. The Steering Committee, because it
is a small body, is not representative of the Labor

Coalition’s full membership. However, because the Steering
Committee has tended to be a principled body, it has adopted
positions which it considered important, and that includes
positions which sometimes are not popular within the wider labor
community .

Due to the above, Directions Committee members unanimously are
reccommending a change in the Labor Coalition by-laws where ali
resolutions, endorsements and public positions must be approved
by the delegates council in order to be adopted. The specific
procedure on adopting positions should include preliminary
approval by the Steering Committee and should then be forwarded
for review and approval at the next General Meeting.

IV. Other Suggestions/Reccommendations
a. Committee members reccommended reinstituting area meetings

b. Ron P. suggested Labor Coalition staff develop a Plan to visit
affiliated local union meetings to talk about the Labor

Coalition and activities. Subject should not be money. No
argument from Chuck W.

Date: April 28, 1995

The war between the Building Trades and the Labor Coali-
tion which, at this writing, seems to be escalating rather
than de-escalating, is not without real casualties. Since
these have not, to my knowledge, been explicitly pointed
out yet, I thought it would be important to do so.

1. Solidarity Ads
Last year the Building Trades members contributed $1,250

in ads to the Solidarity issue of the Working Press. This
obviously will be reduced this year. $450 from Laborers
and Masons is out already; we’ll probably lose another
$500 at least (anybody have other guesses?) for a loss of
$950.

2. Dues

Last year the Building Trades members paid $1,526 in dues.
I don’t know how much we have received so far this year.
We will obviously lose the $265 from the Laborers and
Masons, probably some on top of that from others. lLet’s
estimate the total loss at $500.

3. 1995 Health and Safety
The Trades received a $10,000 grant this year of which the

Labor Coalition is targeted to receive about $6,500 for
training programs, a needs assessment and technical assis-
tance. The program is largely on hold right now. What
happens for the duration of this year is hard to predict
at this point, but it is quite possible that the needs as-
sessment may not happen and technical assistance will be
less than planned. If so it means a loss of at least
$2,000 relative to what we budgeted as income for this

year.

4. 1996 Health and Safety
It is likely that there will be no Building Trades grant

for 1996, immediately lowering our "hoped-for" income for
next year by $5,000. In fact the loss may be much greater
for us (and them). Given the large membership in the

Building Trades unions and the very high risk involved in
construction work, the Building Trades’ potential for
health/safety funding is far higher than the $10,000
ye awarded them in 1995. There is no way to predict this, of
y course, but to put it in perspective: UAW 2300 with fewer

members and less documented risk has received $37,000
three years running.

5. My own feelings of demoralization

Since I had long struggled to establish this program and
these ties with the Building Trades, and since it has been
a great success so far, it feels like a very significant
loss to me. I also feel some personal responsibility for
the conflict that has developed (in not acting more
Strongly to prevent it, as I think it should have been).
It also reinforces a sense that I have that the Coalition
leadership is leading but not enough members are follow-
ing; that our roots and ties with rank-and-file members
are increasingly weak and tenuous; and that this is not
compensated for by our increasingly strong ties with
community groups.

6. 1995 Budget

te Our audit disclosed that the auditee did not correctly report expenses for several
budget lines. The amounts reported for fringe benefits and bookkeeping
expenses contained mistakes that resulted in $1,031.20 being reimbursed for
charges not incurred. The hourly rate reported for the bookkeeper was greater
than the actual rate paid; with the overreimbursement totaling $692.98. In
addition, the auditee, among other errors, included the federal and state income
tax withholdings as part of the fringe benefits expenses. The net overpayment
for this expense category was $338.32. However, there are no questioned costs
as the auditee paid for program expenses that were not reported for

reimbursement.

The auditee incurred expenses of $1,184.26 in the salaries line and other
operating expenses line that exceeded the reimbursement they received. The
reason that these expenses were not paid by the NYSDOL is that they exceed
the budget line for each of the expense categories. A budget modification would

have allowed the auditee to report the actual charges paid.

We recommend that the Midstate Central Labor Council develop procedures to
ensure the accurate reporting of the actual expenses paid on behalf of the OSH
program. In addition, they should monitor the contract's expense lines and

request the appropriate budget modifications.
