Introduction

The labor movement is facing fierce challenges as we approach the new millenium. These
challenges are both external and internal to our union organizations. In the last two decades we
have seen the globalization of corporations and massive restructuring here at home. Corporate
decisions to attack the power of labor have been largely successful and have threatened the ability
of our unions to survive and our communities to prosper. The failure of the US labor movement
to lead American workers and communities to respond is just as much a function of obstacles
internal to labor and progressive social organizations as it is the forces of capital. Through it all,

one fact is clear, the labor movement must inspire and renew its members commitment to
organizing and broaden its social agenda or it will die.

We can no longer run our locals, internationals and labor councils under the outmoded
“service” model. We must change to an “organizing” model and this must be initiated at all levels
and in every corner of the country. The AFL-CIO Union Cities program has provided labor

councils with a blueprint for building strong and vibrant organizations which are integrally
connected to the communities in which they exist.

The goals are simple, yet allow for individual expression which has been a hallmark of the
our labor movement when it is successful: 1) Organizing to Change, Changing to Organize (2)
Mobilizing Against Anti-Union Employers (3) Building Political Power and Community
Coalitions (4) Promoting Economic Growth, Protecting Our Communities (5) Educating Union
Members in Pocketbook Economics (6) Generating Support for the Right to Organize (7)
Making Sure Our Leadership Mirrors the Faces of Our Membership (8) Encouraging All Local
Unions to Increase Their Membership. These goals are bold and aggressive, but on a practical
level, too difficult, if not, impossible for the vast majority of labor councils to intiate.

Building the Road to the Union City is a major undertaking and like any construction
project requires the necessary time, material, equipment and, most importantly, qualified, oe
professional staff. The lack of any one of these elements dooms the proposal to an aC
idea, a project which never becomes a reality. In as much as 15% of the central labor Sy ae
the AFL-CIO are located in small towns, rural areas and geographically fr agmented eee
strategies for implementing the Union Cities program in these areas must bea ati He ?
most of these labor councils will not be able to initiate the Union Cities agenda wit ness 4
assistance of full-time, paid organizers to support, encourage and coordinate the volu
resources of unions and their members in these areas.
SE ASP IOP eS “NTT IAIn#eh. .

Building the Road to the Union City through small towns is as critical as renewing the
infrastructure of the labor movement in a large metropolitan area, How, then, do small labor
councils proceed? Mergers or consolidations into “super councils” are one solution, but this may

reduce the participation and commitment of the member unions in the smallest councils as they
see the program dictated by larger towns or cities.

The Labor Coalition is proposing a different model and asking for the national office to
provide financial assistance on a pilot project basis. Our model is one that respects the integrity,
structure, individuality and demographics of each labor council that would participate. Rather
than merging, we are proposing a collective effort between small labor councils to respond to the
Union Cities program. Call it “networking” or “clustering” the end result is a sharing of ideas,
resources, and costs associated with implementation of the Union Cities program. Because staff
salarjes_gre the largest cost factors and most critical element to implementation of the Union

Cities initiative the networking would start with the “collective” hiring of an organizer to start
building the Road to our Union Towns.

The Labor Coalition, Midstate Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO has recieved strong
indications of support from the Steuben County Labor Council and the Chemung County Labor
Council to undertake this pilot project. We have identified the staff responsibilities, necessary
commitment and a timeline for implementation of the proposal.

and mayors held hostage by employers seeking to expand or threatening
to relocate, and a "hands-off" attitude from Washington which only
fueled the Economic Development Civil War.

Whatever progress that was made on the federal level to help
dislocated workers was the culmination of twenty years of state and
local experimentation, in response to growing public discontent. The
best ideas "trickled up," and that is a hopeful sign that further
improvements will continue under the new Worker Adjustment and
Retraining Notification (WARN) Act and the new Economic Dislocation
Worker Adjustment Assistance (EDWAA) Act. States continue to lead
the way in dislocated worker policy innovations, and we outline here
some of the emerging issues.

The 1990s are the time to build on these early hesitant steps
with policies to improve the performance of economic development
programs and programs to prevent unnecessary plant closings and the
dislocation of workers. We outline several promising methods already
in place at the state level which are gaining wider attention. These
can be the building blocks of an action agenda on a local level that

can lead to a comprehensive and effective national policy.

. Finally, although we have tried to uncover every law relevant to
this subject, there has been a great deal of activity in this field
recently, and we may have missed something. If you have news of
other developments in plant Closings laws or development subsidy

restrictions, we'd like to hear from you.

organizations fighting plant closings and other effects of the U.S. industrial crisis.

After years of waging local battles, the 15 local groups which founded FIRR felt the
time was right to join together to share organizing experiences and strategies and
build a national industrial agenda to save jobs and communities.

THE 1988 PLANT CLOSING LAW

Effective Date: (Section 11)

This law went into effect on February 4, 1989,

Definitions: (Section 2)

"Employer" means any business which employs 100 or more employees, or
whose employees work an aggregate of 4,000 hours per week or more.

"Plant closing" means the permanent or temporary cessation of employment
for 50 or more employees within any 30-day period.

"Mass layoff" means a reduction in workforce of at least 33% and no

less than 50 of the employees during any 30-day period. Such a reduction
can be the loss of employment from termination, a layoff exceeding 6
months or a 50% reduction in hours of work during a 6 month period.

Notice Requirements: (Section 3)

An employer will not close a plant or order a mass layoff until the
end of a 60-day period after a written notice has been given, announcing
such intentions, to the following entities:

All union representatives of the effected employees.

All effected employees, if there is no union representation.

The State dislocated worker unit in that area.

The chief elected official (i.e. mayor, town supervisor or county
board) of the local government within which the intended closing
or layoff is to take place.

Dear Sisters and Brothers:

Representatives from over a dozen unions in Ithaca and Cortland
recently met to explore ways in which they might work together to
promote the mutual concerns of labor in the region. While many sug-
gestions were made to advance the cause of area unions, some of which
are described below, the meeting focused on two topics. First, much
of the evening's discussion centered on the need to establish a joint
body of Ithaca/Cortland labor unions. The second major focus was la-
bor's involvement in the upcoming 1984 elections. A consensus was
reached to give more serious consideration to the idea of forming a
labor council and that this body might initially undertake a project
of political action and education for 1984.

As mentioned above, other concerns were brought up and should be
considered for future action. Among these were suggestions for a li-
brary or resource center which could serve, for example, as a clearing-
house on labor legislation or legal referrals; establishing a labor
newsletter; planning educational programs for school children as well
as programs for our members; and support for each other during nego-
tiations, strikes, or when under attack by union busters.

It was clear from our initial meeting that now is an especially
critical time for labor unions to act in a united fashion. Therefore,
to further work out*the proposals for a labor council and political
action, a meeting for all Ithaca/Cortland unions was called for Tuesday,
March 8 at 6:15 p.m. in the North Room of the Statler Inn on the
Cornell campus. The ILR school will provide dinner for the meeting.
Please let Cathy Todd know by no later than March 6 if you or a rep-
resentative of your union will be able to attend or not. Cathy can

be reached at 256-4423.

For all those present at our last meeting, we look forward to
seeing you or a delegate from your local on March 8. If you have any
further questions concerning the meeting, don't hesitate to call me
at 256-4405 (days) or 277-1285 (evenings).

agenda for the general meeting, to get out pertinent mailings,
to act as spokespersons with the media. Steering committee
meetings will be open for any members of the labor union com-
munity to attend, with voice but not vote, and will be held
two weeks before each general meeting.

II. General meetings

General meetings will be held monthly, and at these meetings
the group will set its policies and approve all action items.
All actions .taken by the steering committee will be subject
to approval by the group at the monthly meetings.

Two voting delgates will be allowed for each member union,
providing that union has paid all assessments and fees.

There will be no absentee ballots. All meetings are open to
any and all members of the labor union community.

\The Tompkins-Cortland Joint Labor Coalition met this evening

in Tompkins and Cortland County. A political action committee has
been formed to explore appropriate ways to involve union members
in local and national politics. The Coalition also hopes to put
on a tremendous LAbor Day bash for workers in all the surrounding
County.

are open to all members of the labor community.

Dear Mr. Watson

I am writing to you concerning the current crises in tke
Ithaca City School District. I write not only as a person active in the
Labor Movement but also as a tax payer and a parent. My son is in the second
grade at South Hill School and my daughter will be a studeht in a few years.

I recently attended a meeting of the Ithaca Teachers Asso.
and saw my son's teacher there in attendence. I realized how, as a parent,
I was so demanding on her skills, committment, time and energy. I also
realized how working without a contract, especially in the present atmosphere
in the District, saps her of her morale, threatens her self respect, and
attacks her dignity as a person and as a professional teacher. As a trade
unionist I am concerned about justice and fair play for the teachers, and
as a father I am angry about conditions that will ultimately effect the
healthy development of my son.

I am disturbed when I hear of the attacks on the old contract.
I am especially concerned when I hear catch phrases like “mandatory evaluations
and “merit pay". These concepts, which are prevalent in anti-union campaigns,
only serve to humiliate the teachers and can never result in quality education.

Most disturbing of all is the fact that members of the School

Board have yet to appear at the bargaining table. As elected officials, how
do you explain this failure to become involved in these talks which are so
vital to our entire community? Many people I've talked to agree with the
view that involvment in the negotiating process by yourself and other members
of the Board can succeed in bringing this long and painful impass to an end.

We recently shared the same platform at the Women's Community
Building. I am asking that you carry that same spirt of hope into this local
struggle. I believe you possess the strength and courage to inspire the Board
to quick and decisive action. I look to you to initiate a free and open
dialogue with the Teachers Asso. And I look to you to protect the hard earned
rights of our very fine teachers. Nothing less than the enrichment of our ‘i
children depends upon your action and good faith.

Sincerely,

Preamble

The establishment of this Local Central Body as a subordinate
unit of the American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial
Organizations is an expression of the desire of the unions in this
community to participate fully in the achievement of the objectives
of the parent Federation as it seeks to fulfill the hopes and aspirations
of the working people of all America.

We seek the fulfillment of these hopes and aspirations through
democratic processes within the framework of our constitutional gov-
ernment and consistent with our institutions and traditions.

At the collective bargaining table, in the community, in the exercise
of the rights and responsibilities of citizenship, we shall responsibly
serve the interests of all the American people.

We pledge ourselves to the more effective organization of working
men and women; to the securing to them of full recognition and en-
joyment of the rights to which they are justly entitled; to the
achievement of ever higher standards of living and working condi-
tions; to the attainment of security for all the people; to the enjoy-
ment of the leisure which their skills make possible; and to the
strengthening and extension of our way of life and the fundamental
freedoms which are the basis of our democratic society.

We shall combat resolutely the forces which seek to undermine the
democratic institutions of our nation and to enslave the human soul.
We shall strive always to win full respect for the dignity of the
human individual whom our unions serve.

With Divine guidance, grateful for the fine traditions of our past,
confident of meeting the challenge of the future, we proclaim this
constitution.

ARTICLE I—Name and Affiliation
This organization shall be known as the

AFL-CIO, hereinafter referred to as the Central Body. It shall at all
times maintain affiliation with the American Federation of Labor and
Congress of Industrial Organizations in accordance with the laws of
that organization. AS A CHARTERED ORGANIZATION OF THE
AFL-CIO THIS CENTRAL BODY SHALL CONFORM ITS ACTIV-
ITIES ON STATE MATTERS TO THE POLICIES OF THE STATE
CENTRAL BODY, AND ON NATIONAL AFFAIRS TO THE
POLICIES OF THE AFL-CIO.

ARTICLE I—Objects

The objects of this Central Body shall be to promote, through
appropriate activities in the geographical area covered by the charter
of the Central Body, the principles of the American Federation of
Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations, including the
following: :

(a) To assist in furthering the appropriate objects and policies of
the AFL-CIO, or of organizations affiliated with the AFL-CIO (pro-
vided such objects or policies are not inconsistent with the objects or
policies of the AFL-CIO) ;

(b) To serve as a means of exchanging information among affili-
ated bodies on matters of common interest; ;
(c) To provide aid, cooperation and assistance to
affilitated local unions and other affiliated bodies in
their common and individual endeavors;

(d) To propose, support and promote legislation favor-
able to and to oppose legislation detrimental to the interest
of workers and organized labor.

(e) To encourage workers to register and vote, to
exercise their full rights and responsibilities of citizen-
ship, and to perform their rightful part in the political
life of the local, state and national communities;

(f) To engage in such other activities as are consis-
tent with the objects and principles set forth in the
Constitution of the AFL-CIO and the policies of the AFL-CIO.

Section 7—Upon acceptance of a delegate’s credential, the presid-
ing officer shall administer the following obligation: “I, [name of
delegate], do solemnly pledge my honor that I will obey the rules ana
regulations of this Central Body and, to the best of my ability, per-
form all the duties I may be called on to discharge as a delegate
thereto. I also pledge that I will patronize only union labels, shop
cards and service buttons when they are available and that I will
qualify myself to vote in all local, state and federal elections.”

Section 8—Absence from three consecutive meetings of the Central
Body without an acceptable excuse shall be sufficient grounds for de-
claring a delegate’s seat vacant, following which the Secretary-Treas-
urer shall notify the delegate’s organization and request that a new
delegate be sent.

to one vote. Voting shall be by voice vote or division of the house
(show of hands or standing vote) unless a roll call vote is properly
demanded by the required number of delegates as provided for
in Sec. 2 of this Article. No delegate shall be permitted to cast
the proxy of another delegate and no delegate shall be allowed to
represent more than one organization.

ARTICLE ViI—Duties of Officers

Section 1—The President shall be the presiding officer of all meet-
ings of the Central Body and of the Executive Board. He shall coun-
tersign all orders for the payment of funds of the Central Body. He
shall exercise general supervision over the affairs and activities of
the Central Body and shall perform such other duties as usually ap-
pertain to the office and as may be ordered by the Central Body or
the Executive Board. He shall have power to interpret this Consti-
tution, subject to ratification of the Central Body. He shall be ex-officio
a member of all committees. He may appoint as many Sergeants-at-
Arms as necessary to assist.in maintaining order and in the conduct of
meetings of the Central Body.

Section 2—(a) The Secretary-Treasurer shall be the custodian ‘of
the records of the Central Body. He shall keep a correct record of the

prospecings of all meetings of the Central Body and of the Executive
3oard.

(b) The Secretary-Treasurer shall receive and disburse all funds of
this Central Body upon proper authorization. He shall maintain ade-
quate financial records showing the standing of all alliliated organiza-
tions and the source and disposition of all funds in his care. He shall
See Rule 11(e¢)

handle the funds and keep the financial records in a manner which will
meet the applicable requirements of the Code of Ethical Practices
concerning accounting and financial controls as approved by the Exec-
utive Council of the AFL-CIO and as may be required by the Secre-
tary-Treasurer of the AFL-CIO under the rules governing local Central
Bodies,

(c) The Secretary-Treasurer shall submit to the Central Body a
monthly financial statement of all funds in his keeping, showing the
accounts in such detail as the Executive Board or the Central Body
may require, and shall submit his books for audit on request of the
Executive Board, but at least annually.

Section 8—The Vice President shall perform the duties of the
President in his absence or incapacity and shall assist the President
when requested.

Section 4—The Trustees shall be the custodians of the physical
properties of the Central Body and shall prepare and maintain an
inventory of all such properties showing the date of purchase, the
cost and estimated current value. They shall examine the records of
the Secretary-Treasurer quarterly and shall report to the Central
Body on the condition of these records.

ARTICLE VIII—Executive Board

Section 1—The Executive Board shall be composed of all the officers
enumerated in Article VI, Section 1.

Section 2—-The Executive Board shall be the governing body of the
Central Body between meetings and it is authorized and empowered
to take such action and render such decisions as may be necessary
to carry out fully the decisions and instructions of the Central Body
and as may be necessary and appropriate to safeguard and promote
the best interests of the Central Body and its affiliated unions.

Section 3—The Executive Board shall meet regularly at least once
each month at such time and place as it may determine and it shall
meet on call of the President when a special meeting is necessary.

Section 4—The Executive Board shall have the power to make a
temporary appointment te any office not otherwise provided for in
this Constitution for the period of a temporary disability or the ab-
sence of an officer or, in case of a permanent vacancy, until a special
election has been held.

Section 5—A quorum for transaction of the business of the Execu-
tive Board shall consist of a majority of its members.

While some of this active collaboration already exists, and some of it awaits

This legislation has three purposes. First, the legislation seeks to promote
the creation and maintenance of jobs for all Ithacans who wish to work.
Second, the legislation seeks to enable the City to respond effectively to
plant closings, relocations, or substantial reductions in workforces. Third,
the legislation seeks to retain and encourage employers within our community
who treat their employees in a reasonable fashion.

To accomplish these purposes the legislation includes three components:

ADVANCE NOTICE

1. All employers will be required to give sufficient advance notice to their
employees and to the City of a closing, relocation, or substantial reduction

in workforce. For employers of 1 to 15 people, 30 days notice will be .
required; :.r employers of 16 to 99 people, 60 days notice will be required;

and, for employers of more than 100 people, 90 days notice will be required.
Failure to provide the notice will be a criminal violation.

REPORTS AND INVESTIGATIONS

2. All employers of 16 or more people who intend to close, relocate, or
substantially reduce their workforce, will be required to provide to the City
a@ report detailing the economic circumstances which lead them to that
decision, thus enabling employers and the City to work together to define
feasible alternatives. If requested, the Mayor shall direct that the City

Planning staff study and report on the possibilities for effective City
action.

CODE FOR RESPONSIBLE EMPLOYERS

3. All employers in the City of Ithaca will be encouraged to sign a Code for
Responsible Employers providing for additional protection for employeees in
the event of a closing, relocation, or substantial reduction. Signature of
the Code would be required of any employer receiving financial assistance,
directly or indirectly, from the City. The Code requires employers, in the
event of a closing, relocation or substantial reduction: to continue any
health insurance plans for employees for up to 3 months after their
employment ceases; to provide up to 2 weeks leave time to employees to enable
them to look for other jobs; and to provide a severance payment equal to the

employee’s weekly wage multiplied by the number of years for which they have
_been employed by the employer.

To the Editor;

A small, loose knit group of employees at Cornell refer to themselves
collectively as "Workers Against Unions." Using the sympathetic Ithaca
Journal as a forum, WAU has expressed a good deal of outrage toward the
United Auto Workers, the union which represents them on the job. while
much of their complaining is desultory and vague, there is one area in
which they are crystal clear: they see a Union Shop clause as an
infringement on their freedom of choice.

I try to avoid the argument which emphasizes the fact that all bar-
gaining unit members, whether or not they join the union, are by law
represented by officers freely elected by their fellow workers. In a
country where citizens feel increasingly alienated from their elected
leaders, cynical about the democratic process, and debilitated by a
general feeling of powerlessness, this argument tends to bring out
the closet monarchist in many. After all, why should I expect people
to want to pay dues and vote when so many pay taxes and still don't vote.

These "Workers Against Unions" simply aren't interested in on the
job democracy, a voice and a vote in the workplace - never were. They
didn't vote for the union and see no reason why they should join, pay
dues, vote or participate in any way. In all fairness to their anger
let's make a few observations from a slightly different perspective.

Before the union there was always a closed shop at Cornell. In
those days all workers were required to belong to Day Hall. To understand
this assertion just remember that if the union had lost their election -
by say a vote of 500 to 400 - the 400 workers who had voted for the union
would still not have been allowed to have one. This Cornell closed shop
was as closed as a shop can get; in this closed shop no worker had a
vote of any kind, and no representation either.

If the WAU feels that management i§ usually on the correct side of
labor/management issues then they should join the union and speak out
and vote accordingly. This gives management a voice in the union hall
while bringing dissent and diversity to the union. This is what democracy
is all about. Without dissent a union becomes a club of pro-union people,
a cult which sees all issues from the same narrow perspective - in other
words an institution greatly resembling management. Surely, this is not
the kind of representation that the employees in WAU deserve.

On 2/18/86 a motion to reconsider moving Department of Social Services

was based on financial data alleging that hospital space could be converted

way the County intends to maintain that low cost is to undercut prevailing
wage laws. The County intends to work on this public project utilizing public
funds by hiring workers to do painting and fix up under the civil services
classification of cleaner at an annual salary of $10,156. Further, the
conversion plan does not provide for compliance with New York State Building
and Fire Code Regulations. The move is vehemently opposed by CSEA, that
maintains that the plan does not meet County space needs responsibly. The
County intends to hide total cost of the project by stringing -it:out over
years and expecting the workers to shoulder the burdens and inconvenience of
such a move with the tax payer ultimately picking up the tax.

local CSEA office, 273-8353. They aré asking people to contact their

Representatives asking for a vote to RESCIND resolutions to move county
offices to the old hospital building.

In a year when the County is already discussing a 20% tax increase
allegedly because of loss of revenue sharing, they found over $90,000 to

convert the hospital to office space. The hospital should be sold, returned
to tax roles and rehabilitated by local labor!

PRESS STATEMENT

Unions Call for Investigation of Smith Corona Lay Offs

Last week the Cortland community was rocked by Smith Corona's
announcement of another major workforce reduction. According to
media accounts and company statements 350 workers were laid off,
some with seniority dating back to 1985. This lay off came on the
heels of another lay off in January of over 100 workers. Tho: of
us in the labor movement who have been figh'' | ° ¥ NG AVS
and improve employment for workers are once again shocked and
disheartened by the acquiescence of the community in the face of
this kind of corporate slaughter.

Today, we, members of this community are expressing our
outrage at what has happened and the way it has happened. We are
pledging ourselves to unite our forces to protect our homes, our
communities and our livelihoods. We are members of labor unions,
environmental groups and community members. We are speaking out
today not simply for Smith Corona workers who were given no notice
of their lay offs, but for all workers, unionized and non-unionized
who are at the mercy of corporate greed.

Smith Corona had no qualms announcing that while they were
throwing 350 Cortland area workers onto the street that they were
employing 300 additional workers in Singapore. There is only one
message in this for Cortland workers and that is "watch out” cause
you are next. If you can't compete with Korean, Mexican and Puerto
Rican workers for the lowest wages and worst working conditions you
can kiss your jobs goodbye.

There is another message for communities like Cortland all
across America and that is "watch out" cause you are next. Our
only allegiance is to money, and whether we make it in Cortland or
Korea makes no difference to us.

Global competition has put communities like Cortland all
across the United States in a dangerously vulnerable position.
Understanding this, the labor movement fought for more than 7 years
for all workers and communities to get restrictions on plant
closings and mass lay offs. Companies like Smith Corona viciously
fought against such legislation. Nevertheless, in April of 1989
the Federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Act (WARN) went into
effect. And while most of us consider this law weak and

ineffective there are some restrictions which corporations must
adhere to or face penalties.

The law requires companies of more than 100 workers, who lay
off 33% of their workforce in a month or in 90 waveeif it is for
the same reason to provide the community and the effected workers
with 60 days notification. There are management consulting firms
traveling the country now training corporations like Smith Corona

how to subvert and avoid obeying the law however. And the

PRESS STATEMENT

During our investigation of massive layoffs at Smith Corona
we gathered information from almost 100 current and former Smith
Corona employees, who helped us piece together a history of plant
operations and workforce reductions since August,1989. What
emerged from their stories is a picture of a company which has
abused its employees. If company statements are accurate, at
least 1000 workers, or 48% of the work force, have been laid-off
since August 1989. Many employees told us they believe the actual
number may be even higher than that.

The layoffs came with little or no advance notice. Most
employees were given 1-5 days notice of permanent layoff, anda
large number of workers were laid-off without any notice. We
heard about lay-offs 8 months short of retirement, pregnant women
laid-off without warning after they had used up part of their
unemployment benefits ina workshare program at the plant, and
people with 18 to 23 years of seniority who were told to go home
when they came to work. These abuses came from a company that
expects 2 weeks notice from employees who quit.

Company representatives have claimed their employees were
told about layoffs as soon as the decisions were made, and that
layoffs were done by seniority and job performance. They also
claimed they were not shifting jobs from Cortland to Singapore.
None of these claims are credible. For example,at a plant meeting
March 20,1990, management assured workers there would not be
layoffs, and the next day they started laying off 350 people.Some
of these workers told us their supervisors had later admitted to
them, off the record, that they had known about the layoffs for
several weeks but had been told to deny the rumors. We were also
told layoffs did not generally reflect seniority, though some
"bumping" by seniority did occur. Many people suggested the
company might actually be targetting high-seniority employees to
avoid retirement costs. It is also clear that the company has
been shifting production from Cortland to Singapore, a process
which surely requires advance planning. Consider the following:

* Between April and August,1989, Smith Corona shifted its basic
'L’ line typewriter to Singapore.

* In Jan.,1990, the company brought workers from Singapore into
the Cortland plant to train them in production of the ’ML’ line
typewriters (SD’s, XL’s,XD’s) . Workers from Singapore were
trained for other jobs in March and April.

* In late March,1990, 350 Cortland workers were laid-off, 300
workers were hired in Singapore, and production of some ML models
(the SD series, and we believe a substantial part of the XL/XD
production) , Shifted to Singapore. Cuts in ML production resulted
in the loss of 4 first shift lines and 2 second shift lines, each
employing about 18 people.

Other production cuts in the plant must also have been
planned in advance. Production in word processors (PWP’s) has
been reduced to one line, and production in plastics, cartridges,
circuit boards, metal operations, and other jobs has been
significantly reduced. The plant is often described by current
employees as a "shell" with only skeleton production and rework

We think we have documented worker abuse at Smith Corona. We
had hoped to bring a suit against the company under the federal
plant closing law (the WARN law), because of their failure to
give 60-days notice of 1

ayoff. What we’ve learned is that the law
is too weak to protect employees, and communities, from the

devastating impact of sudden job losses. Under the law, we must
depend on the company to tell us how many employees have been
laid-off on what dates. If 33% of a workforce is laid-off within
a 30-day period, or a 90-day period for the same cause,
workers must be given 60-days notice. If company statements are
accurate, and we cannot prove they are not, they avoided the
notice requirement by spacing out their layoffs over several
months. We had anticipated that evasion strategy. However, the
law also requires companies to give 60-days notice if even 50
workers are laid-off ina 30-day period as a result of shutting
down an "organizationally distinct" product, operation, or work
function. We had hoped to build a case on the layoffs which
occurred in March,1990, when at least some of the ML typewriters
were shifted to Singapore. Although we think there may have been
a violation of the law at that point, we’ve decided not to bring
a suit because the WARN law does not define the term
‘organizationally distinct product’, so we don’t know if a court
would accept a product line ( such as the SD series) asa
distinct product, or would define it in more generic terms,e.g.
as the entire ML line of typewriters. Although it’s very
difficult for outsiders to get information about products, we
think the company actually changed its original plan to send all
the ML lines to Singapore last year. We were told they kept 2
lines of XL’s & XD’s in Cortland. By keeping a skeleton
production of products while laying off workers companies are
probably safe from the legal obligation to give 60-days notice.
Again, we are disappointed that we were unable to get some
compensation for the workers whose lives have been so seriously
disrupted by sudden job losses. But we hope our efforts will help

panere get a stronger law which will protect our rights in the
uture.

Dear Mr. Chairman,

This letter is submitted in response to your request for
written comments on the operation of the US foreign trade
zone (FTZ) program. We respectfully request that this
letter be included in the printed record of the hearing.
Smith Corona Corporation strongly supports the continuation
of the Foreign-Trade Zone Program as it exists today. It
considers its designation as Foreign Trade Subzone 930A a
significant factor in the extraordinary turnaround it has
achieved since July, 1985. Since that time Smith Corona has
increased production sixfold, more than doubled employment
and has initiated a highly successful export program. Smith
Corona believes that the continuation of the Foreign-Trade
Zone Program is instrumental to its efforts to maintain its
position as the leading manufacturer of portable electronic
typewriters and personal word processors in the globai

market.

Smith Corona Corporation is the world's largest manufacturer |

of portable electronic typewriters and one of the largest
manufacturers of personal word processors. The company also
markets electronic reference products and office supplies.

History

During the early 1980's, due to an influx of low priced
foreign typewriters, Smith Corona, a leader in the field

for decades, saw a substantial decline in marketshare. Asa
result of this loss of sales, Smith Corona incurred two
successive 2 multi-million dollar losses.

industries in the late 1970s. By March 1984, local

First in Smith Corona's recovery plan was the redesign and

(in a record four months) the privilege of cperating as 2
Foreign Trade Subzone. If Smith Corona's application had
not been handled so expeditiously, it is conceivable that

Foreign-Trade Zone Impact

1, 1985, employment levels have climbed steadily to over

Domestic Impact

This return to profitability by one of the largest empioyers

3.7%. It has had a dramatic positive ripple effect not only

production has resulted in significantly higher orders for

PROFILE ON SMITH CORONA LAYOFFS
Possible Violation of the Federal Plant Closing Law (WARN)

Background:

On March 16, 1990 Smith Corona Machine (SCM) announced it
was laying off 350 workers from its Cortland plant. The pink
slips were to be given out that weekend and the following week.

At the same time SCM announced that it was adding 300 jobs
to its plant in Singapore, due to the increased demand for
cheaper products made there.

The March layoff came on the heels of another SCM layoff in
late January of over 100 workers, bringing the total number of
workers laid of within about 60 days to more than 450.

According to laid off workers, some were called at home and
told not to report for work, others received notice when they
arrived at the plant and others were given a few days. It seems
clear that the vast majority of workers were not given even three
days notice before they were shown the door.

Needless to say the layoff took Tompkins and Cortland
Counties and the workers by surprise. There was no time for
contemplation or preparation. In fact, according to some workers
company spokespeople has expressly denied, only the previous
week, that any layoffs would occur.

After learning of the layoffs the Tompkins/Cortland Labor
Coalition (TCLC) decided to look into whether or not SCM had
violated the federal plant closing/mass layoff law. There were a
number of reasons for our decision to look into the matter.

First, the TCLC learned, from national labor sources, that a
Chicago law firm, Seyfarth, Shaw, Fairweather and Geralson, has
been training employers across the country how to avoid the
layoff thresholds which activate the WARN notification
requirements and that many employers are attempting to space
layoffs in such a way as to avoid providing the notification.

The TCLC decided that if SCM was simply trying to avoid the
notification requirements of WARN it would be important to
document. This law is being reviewed this year by Congress and
it will be important to document it's weaknesses and possible
violations with specific cases.

Secondly, the TCLC felt, based on available evidence (news
reports and discussions with workers), it is possible that SCM
violated WARN. Specifically, two sections of the law could have
been violated. The first would be Section 2(a)(2) which defines
a plant closing as "the permanent or temporary shutdown of :
one or more facilities or operating units within a single site of
employment .. . if [it] results in an employment loss .. . for
50 or more employees . .." The second would be Section 3 which
defines a mass layoff as "a reduction in [work] force which
results in an employment loss at the single site of employment

for .. .at least 33 percent of the employees." Neither of
these will be verifiable without an investigation and possibly a
lawsuit. (Smith Corona has no union representing its workers and
therefore access to company records is not possible.)

Thirdly, the TCLC felt compelled to demonstrate the manner

the layoffs are effecting workers, many of whom have been working

Fourth, the TCLC discussed the importance of addressing our
community's, and our country's, vulnerability to the "global
market forces" which now serve to justify much of what business
does. SCM's argument that adding 300 jobs in Singapore is only
coincidental to the reduction of workers here is insulting. Our
communities are being put in direct competition for jobs with
workers in countries where the wage levels are less than a third
of our own and the working conditions are unthinkable here.

SCM has established a plant in Singapore to take advantage
of cheap labor. Clearly, Cortland workers could produce SCM's
cheaper quality typewriters here if the machinery and equipment
had been put here. In 1985 SCM was granted "Free Trade Zone”
status by the federal government. This program is designed to
protect American jobs and while SCM's employment did go up
significantly from 1986 to 1989, they are clearly moving many of
their American operations to Singapore now. In light of this
fact it is important that we face this reality squarely and deal
with it. What is the future for Cortland, Tompkins County or the
hundreds of other communities like ours if we must compete with
third world working conditions.

For all of these reasons, on Monday April 2, 1990 the TCLC
joined with environmental activists (who have fought SCM on their
waste disposal practices)in a press conference to announce our
efforts to look into SCM's actions.

Did SCM Violate WARN?

The WARN 60-day advance notification requirement is
triggered in a number of ways. There are at least three which
may apply to the current SCM situation.

1. A plant closing means the permanent shutdown of one or
more operating units within a single site of employment when it
effects 50 or more workers. [Sec. 2(a)(2)]

2. A mass layoff means a reduction of at least 33% of the
workforce in any 30-day period. [Sec. 2(a)(3)]

3. A mass layoff also means separate layoffs totalling 33%
of the workforce in any 90-day period (unless the employer can
show that the separate layoffs were for separate and different
reasons). [Sec.3(d)]

Based on newspaper reports and information from workers who
have called the TCLC it seems possible that any one of these
three definitions may have been met.

Re: Smith-Corona Layoffs

Dear Coert:

I have been reading WARN ("Worker Adjustment and
Retraining Notification Act") regulations and legislative
history since our meeting on the 28th. As a result, I have
gotten a very different (and more optimistic) sense of what we
may be able to do with the statute. I am writing this letter
to highlight a few of the more interesting things I have
learned and to let you know how I see us as fitting into your
endeavors at this stage of things.

You may remember that an employer has to give notice in
the event of either a "plant closing" or "mass layoff"
involving 50 or more employees. A plant closing is basically
defined as a shutdown of a "Single site of employment" ("SSE")
or of a "facility" or “operating unit" within an SSE. A mass
layoff means a reduction in force at an SSE of either 33% of
the employees or 500 employees. Note that only the SSE (not
the facility or operating unit) matters in the mass layoff
case. That is, you have to lose 33% of the workers at the
whole site to have a mass layoff; 33% of a particular facility
or operating unit won't get you anywhere. For this reason,
you can actually have a plant closing that is too small to be
amass layoff.

What makes things interesting is the way the regula-
tions define SSE, facility, and operating unit.

Lets take SSE first. This is a fairly complicated term
but an SSE is basically a geographically unified physical

For example, suppose there are four operating units at
an SSE, each employing 400 workers. If one of the operating
units is shut down, you have a plant closing. You do not have
a mass layoff, however, because you have lost neither 1/3 of
the work force nor 500 workers.

A Raced gates
| 1 Interim
space devoted to employer operations. If a company has half a
dozen buildings on a single plot of land, it's one SSE. Two
plots of land across the street from one another are still one
SSE. However, two assembly plants on different sides of town,
employing different workers, are separate SSEs. Thus, there
would be no mass layoff if Smith-Corona laid off 350 of 1600
workers at a single industrial park. But change the facts
slightly so that the company lays off 300 of 800 workers at
its "East Side" plant and 50 of 800 workers at its "West Side"
plant and you have a mass layoff at the East Side location.
Therefore, the physical distribution of Smith-Corona plants
and warehouses in and around the City of Cortland becomes
quite important. If they're all together in one spot, we
probably don't have much. If they're spread out a bit,
however, we may have a mass layoff.

The next term is "facility." It basically means
"building." (Again, the term matters for plant closing
purposes but not for mass layoff purposes.) Thus, if the
employer shuts down operations in a whole building, laying off
50 or more workers in the process, you've got yourself a plant
closing.

The final term and the one most difficult to define is
“operating unit." (Again, operating units only come into play
in plant closing situations.) The official definition
contained in the regulations is "an organizationally or
operationally distinct product, operation, or specific work
function within or across facilities at the single site." A
few specific examples are provided to elucidate this defini-
tion: A company's data processing department is an operating
unit but not the smaller sub-units of data entry workers,
computer programmers, etc. An assembly line in an automobile
manufacturing plant is an operating unit. The smaller group
of workers which puts on the doors or bumpers is not. A
particular shift is not ordinarily an operating unit unless it
performs a different operation from the other shifts. Thus,
the third shift in an assembly line is not an operating unit
but the maintenance shift is. Similarly, if a company decides
to contract out security services and lays off the security
force, it has shut down an operating unit. There is obviously
a lot of ambiguity in this concept and things get fuzzy when
it comes to drawing the line between an assembly line, which
usually is an operating unit, and a shift, which normally
isn't, especially in situations where different shifts may
work on different products. In sum, whether a plant closing
has taken place will depend on exactly who was laid off and
exactly what they were doing.

In view of all this, there is a great deal of investi-
gative work that must be done in order to determine whether or
not we have a lawsuit. We need to know (1) the physical
location of every building in which the manufacturing of
product took place, (2) the distribution of workers among the
put ese (3) the organization of workers into assembly
eae s ifts, and other appropriate functional categories
within each building, and (4) the particular products those
workers worked on.

Then, of course, we have to know exactly

where the layoffs occurred within these geographical and
functional categories.

I don't think that we can bring a lawsuit until after
we have obtained fairly strong evidence of a violation. [In
other words, I don't think we can bring a lawsuit blind, for
the purpose of using the suit to gain access to company
records in order to discover if WARN violations have taken
place. There are a number of reasons why I feel this way,
which I would be happy to discuss with you in more detail, but
I will mention at least one which I learned about in the
course of my research: In a WARN lawsuit, the judge may award
attorney's fees, not just to a prevailing plaintiff, but to
the prevailing party, i.e., to whichever side wins. This
means that if we bring an "exploratory" suit and there turns
out to be nothing there, there is potential liability on the
part of TCLC, if named as a party, and/or the individual named
plaintiffs, which could amount to many tens of thousands of
dollars. On the other hand, we could use a small WARN
violation of whose existence we were reasonably certain to
bring the lawsuit and then explore for additional violations
involving other workers. For example, if we knew that Smith-
Corona had completely shutdown a "facility" housing 75
workers, we could use that as the basis for launching the

litigation, hoping to discover evidence of further violations
as the suit progressed.

Mimi and I have discussed our possible role in this

call upon the kind of "“lawyerly" skills we possess. What we

investigation and gather the data, bringing it to us at the
end to analyze from a legal point of view and determine if it

This is an unusual provision, born of the compromises

most statutes where the plaintiff can get attorney's fees, the

Anyway, these, basically, are our thoughts to date. We

Duty to bargain

The employer must bargain with the union "in good faith” over
"terms and conditions" of employment. The union has the
exclusive right to bargain for all employees in the negotiating
unit.

"Good faith" means that the employer must "approach the
bargaining table with a sincere desire to reach an agreement”.
Refusing to bargain in good faith is an "improper practice” under
the Taylor Law, §209-a.2(b). The following examples can serve as
evidence of bad faith intentions:

- Refusing to supply information requested by the union and
necessary for bargaining.

- Refusing to meet at reasonable times, or attempting to dictate
who or how many may be on the union team.

—~ Refusing to abide by ground rules.

- Attempting to bargain directly with the membership instead of
bargaining with the negotiating team.

- Attempting to discourage membership support for the union
through threats, promises, punishment, or discrimination.

- Withdrawing approval of particular parts of the contract on
which the two sides had already reached tentative agreement.

Refusing to negotiate over a mandatory subject of bargaining.
Making unilateral changes in mandatory bargaining subjects

before bargaining to impasse or without talking to the
union (unless the union has waived the merent) .

- Refusing to negotiate over the effects of unilateral changes in
non-mandatory subjects.

- Wages and salaries

B. Program Design and Implementation: This program is designed to assist in the

elimination of needless occupational health and safety hazards in the workplace.
This will be done through a combination of projects.

: The training conference topics have been identified because of the numerous
inquiries made by local workers and unions. Clerical workers have expressed
concern about ergonomic and health problems they have experienced using VDT's;
and custodial workers have expressed concern about rashes, burns, nausea and
dizziness associated with cleaning chemicals they use. These concerns have

been verified through OSHA Log Forms obtained in unionized workplaces.

The individualized work with four unions will focus on issues particular
to their worksites. UAW #1326 will focus on building a health and safety
committee, training that committee on locals, state and federal laws, identi-
fication of plant problems, - ; oar ey ak -. and working
with management to address identified problems. UAW #802 will focus on building
a health and safety committee, training that committee on local, state and
federal laws, identification of plant problems and working with management
to address identified problems. UAW #2300 will focus on identifying problems
in the dining areas of Cornel] University. Based on numbers of workers and
OSHA Log Forms accidents in the dining areas pose a significant risk for this
union local. Teamsters #65 will address the problems associated with cement
mixing and delivery. These workers complain of rashes, breathing problems and
physical accidents. Each of thes unions want to focus on health and safety
concerns which are unique to their workplace.

Project Title: Health and Safety Training Program

A. Goals & Objectives:

substances related to custodiai occupations. The project will increase the
awareness of workers to these hazards and encourage their active participation
in activities which will bring these hazards to the attention of management and
labor. Further, the Health and Safety Training Program will concentrate on the
problems of two local unions, United Auto Workers Local # 2300 and Teamsters

Local # 65. Both unions want to focus on health and safety concerns which may be

B. Program Design/ Implementation:

GOAL # 1:

To educate workers in Tompkins and Cortland counties about occupational hazards

associated with asbestos and hazardous cleaning/maintenance substances used in
custodial and housekeeping occupations.

Objective # 1: To hold at least one 2 to 4 hour training workshop on both

of the above stated hazards with 15 to 30 workers from occupations effected
by these specific problems. Technical expertise for these training workshops
will be obtained from organizations such as Cornell University's Chemical

Hazard Information Program (CHIP) and/or the Central New York Council on
Occupational Safety and Health (CNYCOSH).

Objective # 2: To aggressively work with at least five (5) different unions

(see Objective # 5) to obtain their membership's participation and attendance
at the workshops listed in Objective #1. To have three (3) or more trainees
from each union participate in the workshops.

Objective # 3: At the completion of each training workshop, the Training
Coordinator will assist trainees from each union to present the informa-
tion they have learned to the membership of their local unions.

Objective # 4: In conjunction with participating unions, to produce an
easy-to-read brochure about specific health and safety hazards which
should be of concern to their members. The brochure will be oriented to-
ward problems experienced by workers at specific worksites.

Objective # 5: To raise the level of health and safety awareness among
union members by assisting local unions to develop a plan for the dissemi-
nation of training materials listed in Objective #

Objective # 6: To work with unions, including the following, to train
their members on the following hazards:

A. Asbestos and its' potential hazards.

B. Hazardous substances used by cleaning and custodial employees.
(American Postal Workers Union Local # 1151, Cornell Security Em-
ployees Association, International Association of Machinists Local #
4607, Service Employees International Union Local # 200A)

To assist 250 dairy workers represented by Teamsters Local # 65, to identif

Objective # 1: To conduct at least two 2 hour group interviews with dairy

blems associated with their employment. The intervies will focus on working

Objective # 2: To confer with experts, from organizations such as CHIP

safety hazards at their job sites and to determine the extent of the risks
faced by the employees.

Objective # 3: To conduct at least two 2 to 4 hour training workshops with
10 to 20 dairy workers who have been interviewed. At least 2 workers from
each dairy represented by Teamsters Local # 65 will attend the training
workshops and relay this information to other workers at the different
dairies. Professional and technical expertise to develop the training work-
shops will be secured from such groups as CHIP and/or CNYCOSH.

GOAL # 3:

To assist United Auto Workers Local # 2300 with development of a comprehensive
program to deal with health and safety concerns of its' 900 members employed at
Cornell University. Because of the diverse tasks performed by the UAW members
the health and safety program will focus on 2 distinct occupational groupings.

A comprehensive survey of 140 laboratory attendants/custodians and 60 farmhands/
groundscrew will be conducted.

Objective # 1: To conduct a telephone/questionnaire survey of laboratory
zattendants/custodians and farmhands/groundscrew to identify health and
safety problems which are unique to their employment.

Objective # 2: To conduct at least four 2 hour group interviews with labora-
tory attendants/custodians in the Agricultural and Veterinary Schools to
identify health and safety problems associated with their employment. These
employees may have unique concerns, since their worksites are experimental
research laboratories. Research conducted in the laboratories, and to which
the employees are associated, include: animal diseases, plant mutation, gene-
tic research, and other clinical-type research.

Objective # 3: To conduct at least two 2 hour group interviews with farm-
hands/groundscrew from different worksites to clarify and identify health
and safety problems associated with their employment. These employees are
required to work with different types of pesticides and chemicals, which
May be hazardous to their health.

State, University, and UAW documents to further identify and clarify
health and safety hazards associated with occupa

related injury and illness among the 15,000 unionized workers in
our 45 member unions and the 75,000 non-unionized workers in our

evaluate and protect themselves against workplace hazards, and by
helping form, train and improve the effectiveness of health and

safety committees, we seek to empower workers to reduce
workplace hazards and injuries.

1. Training Workshops

Two two-hour workshops are planned with an expected atten-
dance of twenty at each. Each workshop will follow a participa-

and the use of audio-visual aids. They will take place at the
Cortland American Legion Hall, a site we have used in the past.
Using the media, Union communication channels and other means,

Iv. Office and Clerical Workers

8. Health and Safety Newsletter for Office Workers

We plan to produce and distribute four issues, 2,750 copies
each, Of FYI: A Health and Safety Newsletter for Office Workers.
About half of the total copies are mailed or distributed to non-
union employees. It has proven to be extremely popular and a very
valuable and cost effective way to get critical health and safety
information to large numbers of workers, many of whom have no
union representation. In this way we can reach much larger
numbers of workers than we could with more traditional training
programs. The main objective of FYI is to educate office employ-
ees about work-related hazards, so they are better able to
identify the hazards, the ways they can be controlled, and other
sources of information and help.

FYI is not only a unique source of easily accessible and
usable health and safety information for office workers. It also
allows groups of office workers in disparate workplaces to
network among each other. The networking occurs not only because
information on different workplaces is included in FYI, but also
because it is produced through the collective effort of a number
of office workers, working with MCLC staff. Staff and volunteers
join to write and design each issue of FYI, using desktop pub-

lishing software.

Subject areas span the range of topics impacting on worker
safety and health. Future topics include hazard communication
requirements for office workers; VDTs and vision safety; build-
ing-related illness; multiple chemical sensitivity and others.

Office workers have no other source for the information
provided in this newsletter. Because of its uniqueness and
value, we will continue efforts to make FYI available to other
unions, COSH groups, occupational health clinics and other
organizations around the State that are interested in distribut-
ing it to groups of office and clerical workers.

v. School Employees
10. Health and Safety Newsletter for School Employees

1 The four counties served by our central labor council
include about 15 unions representing approximately 3,500 K-12
school employees. There are, in addition, a large number of non-
unionized day care center and other school employees within our
jurisdiction. None of these school employees, whether union or
otherwise, have a regular source of information and education on
health and safety issues affecting themselves. This is our
objective in publishing FYI: A Health and Safety Newsletter for
School Employees.

With assistance from a volunteer group of school employees,
and using our extensive experience producing newsletters, we will
produce three issues of a four-page quarterly health and safety
newsletter for school employees. Working with the unions and
county day care councils, we will distribute this to 5,000 school
employees. Working with PTA. councils in the various school
districts, we will seek also to distribute this newsletter to
parents, a group that has a critical interest in school safety
and health, with an estimated 500 parents receiving it.

Most of the people getting this newsletter have very little
information relating to school health and safety, so this wali] be
a critical resource to them, and is the main objective in pub-
lishing it. The newsletter, in addition, will serve to link
school employees from all the districts and unions in our region,
thus providing a health and safety network that is sure to

provide important benefits in the future.

We have already produced three issues of this health and
safety newsletter (under our 1994-95 OSHTEP project). Topics
covered include indoor air quality, workplace violence, art and
craft hazards in the schools, carbon dioxide testing, pesticides,
and the high rate of breast cancer among teachers. Future topics
include: lab safety, radon, asbestos in schools, electromagnetic
fields, safety issues for school bus drivers.

Because MCLC already produces FYI, we have some infrastruc-
ture in place: the necessary computer skills and equipment ;
experience in writing, graphics and desktop publishing; contacts
with printers; understanding about distribution; a clear idea of
costs and time. We expect to liaise with the following for addi-

Managerial Summary

Scope of Examination

We have examined the financial records and reports of the Tompkins Cortland
Labor Coalition for the period July 1, 1988 through June 30, 1990. The
general objectives of our examination were to determine whether the
financial statements of the auditee fairly present the cash position and
results of financial operations and whether the entity has complied with
laws and regulations that may have a material affect upon the financial
statements.

Background

This audit covers the contract agreements between NYSDOL and the Tompkins
Cortland Labor Coalition. NYSDOL reimbursed the auditee $69,487 to
administer this Occupational Safety and Health Training and Education
Program, Contracts No. 004972 and No. 005402 funded by the General Fund of
New York State. Reported expenditures for the audit period were $69,487.

Major Observations and Conclusions

Our audit disclosed that the auditee was in general compliance with
applicable State laws, regulations, and procedures. The financial reports
of the Tompkins Cortland Labor Coalition present fairly the results of
financial operations and cash position for the period examined except for
the following departures from prescribed State fiscal policy:

1. The auditee did not maintain a documented cost allocation plan to
support the distribution of certain joint expenses between programs.
This resulted in $3,747.75 of questioned costs.

2. The auditee incorrectly reported certain fringe benefit costs. This
resulted in questioned costs of $668.02.

3. The auditee incorrectly allocated rent. This resulted in $90.00 of
questioned costs.

4. The auditee did not provide a clear audit trail for reported program
costs. No questioned costs resulted from this finding.

The total questioned cost is $4,505.77.

It was determined that the findings outlined above did not materially
affect the financial reports submitted to NYSDOL.

The objective of internal accounting and administrative control is to
provide reasonable, but not absolute, assurance as to the safeguarding of
assets against loss from unauthorized use or disposition, and the
reliability of financial records for preparing financial statements and
maintaining accountability for assets. The concept of reasonable assurance
recognizes that the costs of a system of control should not exceed the
benefits derived and also recognizes that the evaluation of these factors
necessarily requires estimates and judgments by management.

There are inherent limitations that should be recognized in considering the
potential effectiveness of any system of internal and administrative
accounting control. In the performance of most control procedures, errors
can result from misunderstanding of instructions, mistakes of judgment,
carelessness or other personal factors. Control procedures whose
effectiveness depends upon segregation of duties can be circumvented by
collusion. Similarly, control procedures can be circumvented intentionally
by management with respect to the estimates and judgments required in the
preparation of financial statements.

Further, projection of any evaluation of control to future periods is
subject to the risk that the procedures may become inadequate because of
changes in conditions and that the degree of compliance with the procedures
may deteriorate.

Our study and. evaluation made for the limited purposes set forth in the
first paragraph of this report would not necessarily disclose all material
weaknesses in the system nor all deviations from prescribed compliance
requirements because it was based on selective tests of accounting records
and related data. Accordingly, we do not express an opinion on the system
of internal accounting control. However, our study and evaluation
disclosed no condition that we believe to be a material weakness.

application of this basis should be uniform and consistent.

Our audit disclosed that the Tompkins Cortland Labor Coalition
incorrectly reported certain fringe benefit costs in Contract No.
005402. Based on our analysis of the actual fringe benefit billings,
we determined that FUTA and disability insurance were underreported and
health insurance was overreported. This resulted in questioned costs
of $668.02. See Auditor’s Exhibit I-B for details.

We recommend that the Tompkins Cortland Labor Coalition report fringe
benefit costs based on actual expenditures per current policies and
billings. In addition, the fringe benefit costs reported should be
restricted to the wage allocation percentages of the staff.

Our audit disclosed that the Tompkins Cortland Labor Coalition
incorrectly allocated rent. The rent expense for three months was
misallocated to the contract. This misallocation totalled $90.00 and
is questioned. See Auditor's Exhibit I-C for details.

We recommend that the Tompkins Cortland Labor Coalition implement
procedures to ensure all costs are properly allocated and reported.

Our audit disclosed that the Tompkins Cortland Labor Coalition did not

provide a clear audit trail for reported program expenditures. The
official books of entry were monthly financial reports which summarized
the entire agency’s checkbook activity. There were no worksheets

provided to reconcile the contract's expenses recorded on the official
books with the expenditures reported on the reimbursement vouchers
‘submitted to NYSDOL. Due to the lack of reconciliation procedures, it
is possible that not all program costs were reported.

Based on our analysis of the contract budget, payroll register and
invoices, we determined the costs reported on the reimbursement
vouchers to be reliable. As a result, the vouchers were used as the
basis for our audit. From our analysis of vouchered amounts, no
material discrepancies were disclosed.

We recommend that the Tompkins Cortland Labor Coalition develop and
implement controls and procedures that would provide a clear audit
trail from the official books of entry to the reimbursement vouchers
submitted to NYSDOL. This system should provide a reconciliation of

SUMMARY: HEALTH AND SAFETY TRAINING WORKSHOPS, JUNE 1990

Safet en two hour training sessions were held in June for Union Health and
y Committee members, stewards and officers, and anyone else interested

in on-the-job safety and health. The twenty-eight participants (some came

to both sessions) included members of seven unions (UAW 1326, IAM 1607, UAW

2300, CSEA 855, CSEA 605, UAW 1774, UAW 802) and one from a nonunion
workplace (J.M.Murray Ctr.).

The first session, entitled Workplace Hazards: Physical, Chemical and
Biological, was led by Jim Platner, Director of the Chemical Hazard
Information Program of the New York State School of Industrial and Labor
Relations, Cornell University. Jim focused on the routes of entry of
chemicals into workers' bodies, how various toxic chemicals affect our
bodies, ways to recognize these hazards and effective ways to protect
workers, including finding alternatives to toxic chemicals. Participants
had questions specific to their own workplaces and to using their unions,
and state and federal laws to secure safer, more healthy workplaces.

The second session, Getting Action to Improve Worker Health and
Safety, included discussions by Louise DeJohn of the Communications Workers
of America in Syracuse, and Lin Nelson and Bob Tompkins of Central New York
Council on Occupational Safety and Health. Louise described how to design
and use 2 workplace health/safety survey to uncover workplace hazards, how
to use the Hazard Communication Standard, and the importance of record
keeping, with many illustrations from her union's experience. Bob expained
a number of state and federal laws with which workers have successfully
secured safer and healthier working conditions, with more detail about the
HCcS and Right to Know laws. Lin outlined examples of linking workers'
actions for a safe and healthy workplace with local community concerns
around environmental issues, and the impact of politics on workers’ health
and safety. Participants discussed various ways their unions have secured
safer and more healthy workplaces, including their use of laws and the
grievance process to enforce workers’ rights. Their questions centered on
strategies and techniques to use, interpretations of laws, and requests for
more information on specific chemicals.

period.

and edited, and then used as a very effective adjunct to the

training sessions.

injury problems at SUNY-Cortland; stress and office workers;
carpeting; VDTs - a summary wall chart; office humidity; overwork;
toners; chair height and design; and fire safety. Each issue
contained the regular "Did You Know" feature.

approximately 700 copies to unionized office workers and 750 to

UAW 1326 (Pall Trinity, August). Nine workers attended this
training workshop dealing with getting action on health and safety

issues.

Staff and parents from 18 area schools and unions, attended this
major training conference. TCLc health/safety trainers were joined
by Greg Siwinski, Industrial Hygienist with the cny Occupational
Health Clinica] Center, as presenters. The main focus was on

Workers Compensation Training Workshop (June). Thirty-nine People,
from eighteen trade unions, eight non-union workplaces, and one
COSH group attended. Both public and private sector workplaces

attorney. A 45 minute overview of the system was followed by 90
minutes of questions.

Workers Memorial Da
morxers Memorial Day

Day this year. Our memorial service and OSHA reform rally was
attended by 75 people, and included representatives from at least
fifteen local unions. The service was dedicated to the 25 Hamlet
fire victims. aA moment of silence was publicly observed at 2 pm

District Attorney Meetings on Workplace Health and Safety Crime

Workers Memorial Day this year was also an occasion on which
the labor movement in Central NY opened a new front in our
campaign for safe jobs. Labor delegations met in separate hour
long meetings with the District Attorneys of Tompkins County,
Cortland County and Schuyler County, all on April 28.

The purpose of these meetings was to discuss the possibility
of local criminal prosecution of employers in cases in which
their negligence and willful violation of safety rules leads to
serious workplace injury or illness.

The meetings served to educate the local prosecutors about the
issue of workplace crime, and about the importance of
prosecution of wrongdoers under the state criminal code. Each
meeting resulted in a commitment by the prosecutors to initiate
investigations and pursue such cases where sufficient evidence
that a worker death or serious injury resulted from negligence
or willful violations was brought to their attention. They also
expressed willingness to continue the dialogue with labor on
this issue. We were encouraged by their response.

HEALTH AND SAFETY TRAINING PROGRAM

Program Summary

This program is designed to assist in the elimination of
needless occupational health and safety hazards. This will be done
through a combination of activities:

training workers to identify, evaluate and protect themselves
against workplace hazards;

helping unions address workplace hazards and improve the
effectiveness of their safety and health committees;

implementing projects designed to reduce work-related
accidents and back injuries.

Program Design: Goals and Objectives
Activity I

ASSIST WORKERS TO IDENTIFY, EVALUATE AND PROTECT THEMSELVES
AGAINST WORKPLACE HAZARDS

GOAL #1: To educate office and clerical workers in Tompkins and
Cortland Counties about the occupational health and safety hazards
associated with office and clerical works and etosifrain these
workers about ways to reduce these hazards.

OBJECTIVE #1: To involve office and clerical workers in the
production and dissemination of a quarterly office workers
health and safety newsletter with a circulation of

approximately 1250.

OBJECTIVE #2: To expand connections between groups of
clericals, unorganized and organized, to further their efforts
to resolve health and safety problems.

OBJECTIVE #3: To conduct training sessions on an as needed
basis, dealing with the occupational hazards in office and
clerical situations, such as video display terminal usage,
stress and indoor air pollution.
OAL #2: To educate teachers, school aides and other staff in area
schools about the health hazards in schools, and to assist these
workers in identifying ways to reduce these hazards.

OBJECTIVE #1: To hold a training conference dealing with the
health and Safety hazards in the schools. This conference
will be organized in conjunction with area unions, including
the Ithaca Teachers Association (NEA), the Cortland Union of
Teachers (AFT), the BOCES Employees Association, CSEA 812,
CSEA 855, and others.

GOAL #3: To Provide access to important health and safety

information to the general workforce in Tompkins and Cortland
Counties,

OBJECTIVE #1: To maintain and further develop a health and
safety resource center for use by workers in the two county
area. To respond to requests for assistance from individual
workers with health and safety concerns, and to act gas-.a
resource and referral service for these workers.

OBJECTIVE #2: To Provide on a regular basis articles on
important health and safety concerns for publication in the
Labor Coalition newspaper, as well as in other union

Coalition newspaper is distributed through Union channels to
7,000 workers in the two counties.

Activity II
ASSIST WORKERS TO IMPROVE THE EFFECTIVENESS OF THEIR HEALTH AND

SAFETY COMMITTEES AND TO ADDRESS WORKPLACE HAZARDS

GOAL #4: To assist in the formation and Ongoing effectiveness of
Union health and safety committees.

OBJECTIVE #1: To assist 175 forge workers represented by UAW
Local 1774 to strengthen their newly-formed union health and

safety committee, We will work with the committee on an
ongoing basis:

to ensure its effectiveness;
to maximize Participation by the rank-and-file;

to help create or strengthen mechanisms for resolving
health and safety Problems;

to help committee members gain access to the information
and resources they need;

to provide training on an as needed basis.
OBJECTIVE #2: To assist other unions, as needed, who are
interested in establishing health and safety committees, or
who need help with the ongoing work of their committees.

OBJECTIVE #3: To develop and hold a Health and Safety Rep
Training course. This course will meet for four sessions and
cover such topics as: understanding and getting information
on workplace hazards: the regulatory framework for health and
safety; health and safety committees; contract language for
health and safety; getting action on health and safety
problems. This course will seek to train ten to twenty Health
and Safety Reps.

Activity III
ASSIST WORKERS TO REDUCE WORKSITE HAZARDS AND BACK INJURIES
GOAL #5: To provide assistance to at least three unions to reduce

worksite hazards and back injuries.

OBJECTIVE #1: To conduct three worksite training sessions for
workers represented by each of these unions.

OBJECTIVE #2: To work with the Unions to identify needed
changes in work design to reduce the possibility of back
injury, and to assist them in bringing these issues before
management.

WILL THE SIDE AGREEMENTS MAKE
NAFTA FAIR TO WORKING PEOPLE?

Trade unions, environmental groups, and citizen organizations have
organized against the proposed North American Free Trade Agree-
ment (NAFTA). These groups are concerned that passage of NAFTA
will result in the loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs and drive down
workers’ living standards. Numerous commentators have described
as "deplorable," the environmental mess created by North American
corporations in the "maquiladora zone," mostly located in Northern
Mexico.

The present Administration has negotiated "side agreements" to the
NAFTA with Mexico and Canada which it believes solves these
problems. This meeting will take a look at the "side agreements.”
We will discuss whether this "new NAFTA" should be supported by
trade unionists and working people.
